title: Fine-tuning for accuracy: evaluation of Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) for automatic assignment of International Classification of Disease (ICD) codes to clinical documentation
headline_numbers: Mean per-code accuracy (target code present in the model's returned code list, MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries, top-10 most prevalent ICD-10 codes, 100 test notes per code = 1,000 test notes): base GPT-3.5 Turbo 29.7%; after fine-tuning on 1,000 notes (100 per code) 62.6%. Per-code base range 10% (Z87891) to 59% (I10); fine-tuned range 33% (Z7901) to 82% (I10); absolute improvement 5-52 points.

i1.basis: Searched Abstract, Methods ("The dataset", "The model", "Evaluating the base model", "Model fine-tuning and evaluation"), Results, Table 4 and Discussion: the only comparator reported anywhere is the default (non-fine-tuned) GPT-3.5 Turbo vs. the fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Turbo. No constant/prevalence/always-emit-top-K predictor is computed. This matters because the evaluation is defined as "For each specific ICD code under review, we verify whether it appears in the model's list for each corresponding note" on notes selected for carrying that code, so a note-blind predictor that always emits the 10 most prevalent codes would score 100% and is never reported.

i2.basis: Searched Methods, Results (Table 4) and Discussion: no TF-IDF/SVM/logistic-regression/CAML/LAAT/PLM-ICD/MSMN/MultiResCNN baseline was re-run or quoted on this split. The Literature review does quote "PLM-ICD had a consistent accuracy of 22%, while GPT-4 accuracy was 22.5% as represented by F1-score (27)" and Huang et al. (3), but those are different datasets (MIMIC-III / other setups) and a different metric (F1), cited as background rather than compared against the paper's own 29.7%/62.6% numbers on its own 1,000-note MIMIC-IV test set.

i3.basis: Searched Methods and Results: the pipeline is a single stage (whole note -> GPT prompt -> code list); there is no retrieval or candidate-generation step, and no oracle/upper-bound, random-selection null, or stage-wise error attribution is reported. Results contain only per-code accuracy (Table 4) for base vs. fine-tuned model.

i4.basis: Searched Methods ("The model", "Evaluating the base model", "Model fine-tuning and evaluation"), Table 1 (dataset summary statistics) and Table 3 (prompt example). The paper gives the prompt template ("Assign ICD-10 codes to the following discharge summary: {Discharge Summary}") and says notes were passed "one-by-one", but never states the context-window size or GPT-3.5 Turbo variant (4k vs 16k), max tokens, temperature, any truncation policy, or note length/token statistics; Table 1 reports only codes per summary, not note size.

i5.basis: Searched Methods ("The model") and Results: a single model is used throughout - "Therefore, we decided to use the GPT-3.5 Turbo model, which would be the latest model offered by OpenAI that can be fine-tuned." The only manipulation is base vs. fine-tuned; input context/form is held fixed (one full discharge summary, one fixed prompt), so no crossed context x capacity design exists.

i6.basis: The system performs no retrieval and displays no evidence: Methods describe passing each note directly to the API ("we passed the notes from the testing dataset one-by-one to the GPT-3.5 model via an OpenAI API and prompted it to assign a list of ICD-10 codes based on the information in each note"). Output is a bare code list (Table 3), so provenance of retrieved evidence cannot apply.

i7.basis: The system makes no evidence or grounding claim - no rationales, quotes, or spans are requested or produced; the output is only "a list of ICD-10 codes assigned to the provided note" (Methods, Table 3), and the sole metric is presence/absence of the target code. Searched Methods, Results and Discussion for span overlap, quote matching, or human adjudication of evidence: none.

i8.basis: The model is prompted for a structured list of codes (fine-tuning target shown in Table 3 as "['M1612', 'E871', 'I10', ...]"), but searched Methods, Results and Discussion for any malformed/unparseable/missing-response rate: none is reported. Scoring is described only as "We then checked if the target ICD-10 code was present in the returned response or not." The nearest remark is a qualitative Discussion note that "the consistency of the content of the model's response for the exact same prompt and summary passed to it may vary", which is not a parse-failure rate. Denominators stay at 100 notes per code, so no exclusion of unparseable outputs is documented.

i9.basis: There is no statistical analysis subsection anywhere; searched Methods, Results and Discussion for bootstrap, permutation, McNemar, Wilcoxon, P values or confidence intervals - none appear. Results report only raw percentages and Table 4 min/max/mean. "Significantly" is used colloquially (e.g. "fine-tuning ... will improve significantly as shown by our study"), which does not count.

i10.basis: Searched Methods, Results, table footnotes, Acknowledgments and Footnote/Ethical Statement sections for any statement about tables or numbers being generated from stored artifacts or checked. The only mention of tooling is dataset preparation - "With Python code, for each of the top 10 most prevalent code, we selected 200 notes randomly" - which concerns sampling, not table provenance; no code/data availability or reproducibility statement accompanies the result tables.

note: Access: complete open-access HTML from the AME/JMAI site (article/view/9040/html), covering Abstract, Highlight box, Introduction, Background, Literature review, Methods (The dataset / The model / Evaluating the base model / Model fine-tuning and evaluation), Results, Tables 1-4, Figures 1-3 captions, Discussion, Conclusions, Footnote and References. Figures are images and their internal numbers were not machine-readable, but Figure 3 is stated to summarise the same base-vs-fine-tuned comparison already given in Table 4, so no scored item hinges on unread figure content. Two items are NA (6, 7) because the design is a direct prompt with no retrieval and no evidence output. The single most consequential gap is item 1: the accuracy definition ("For each specific ICD code under review, we verify whether it appears in the model's list") is evaluated on notes pre-selected to carry that code, with no negative notes and no note-blind floor, so a trivial predictor emitting the ten most prevalent codes for every note would score 100% against the reported 62.6%. Item 8 is coded N rather than NA on the reading that the model is asked for a list-structured output (Table 3); if a scorer treats free-text substring matching as "no structured object", NA would be the alternative, but no parse-failure statistic is reported either way.

title: Developing an ICD-10 Coding Assistant: Pilot Study Using RoBERTa and GPT-4 for Term Extraction and Description-Based Code Selection
source_url: https://formative.jmir.org/2025/1/e60095 (full text obtained as PDF from https://documentserver.uhasselt.be/bitstream/1942/45888/2/xx.pdf; also PMC11835781)
headline_numbers: Lead-term NER (RoBERTa, CodiEsp-X-lead): F1 0.80 combined, 0.82 diagnoses only. Own textual-evidence NER baseline: F1 0.65. End-to-end CodiEsp-X explainability F1 0.305 (diagnoses 0.457, procedures 0.204) vs quoted SOTA 0.633 (FLE 0.611, IAM 0.611). Stage-wise F1 cascade: 0.824 -> 0.509 (step 2) -> 0.378 (step 4 RAG) -> 0.30 (step 5 selection). Retrieval failures @50 on 25 docs/507 codes: diagnoses 160->141 (42.1%->37.1%), procedures 97->91 (76.4%->71.7%) when querying with GPT-4-invented descriptions instead of raw textual evidence. GPT-4 parametric knowledge: 52% of generated descriptions matched official ones; 47% of codes correctly matched to official descriptions.

i1.basis: Searched Methods (GPT-4, Dataset CodiEsp, Dataset CodiEsp-X-lead, Approach, Steps 1-5, Evaluation), Results, both tables, and the whole Discussion; grepped the full text for 'most frequent', 'majority', 'prevalence', 'trivial', 'constant', 'random'. The only item labelled 'baseline' is 'Textual evidence diagnoses and procedures combined (ours-baseline) [29]', a fine-tuned RoBERTa NER model that reads the note; all other comparators are CodiEsp challenge systems. No constant/label-prevalence/most-frequent-code predictor anywhere.

i2.basis: "In step 5, GPT-4 selects the final answer from the retrieved codes, but another drop in performance is observed, resulting in a final F1-score of 0.3 on CodiEsp-x, compared with the SOTA score of 0.633 (Table 2) [5]." Table 2 ('Comparison of performance of different models in the CodiEsp challenge') quotes FLE (0.679/0.514/0.611), IAM (0.687/0.522/0.611) and BETO-Galen+mBERT-Galen+XLM-R-Galen (0.633) against 'Ours' (0.457/0.204/0.305) on the same benchmark, and Table 1 quotes 'Textual evidence diagnoses (SOTA) [5] 0.71'. The authors also re-ran their own supervised comparator on the same split: "The base model from Step 1 was fine-tuned to extract textual evidence solely for benchmarking, achieving an F1-score of 0.65 on the CodiEsp-X test set (Table 1)."

i3.basis: "To assess performance loss at each step, predictions were replaced with actual values in subsequent steps only if the predictions at the current step were accurate." and "In the code retrieval step, the predicted code was replaced with the actual code if the predicted code was among the top-k results." This oracle-substitution cascade is reported per stage in Figure 4 ('F1-Score performance loss for each individual step in the approach') and in the text: "a significant drop in explainability F1-score was observed, falling from 0.509 to 0.378" and "the explainability F1-score dropping from 0.378 to 0.3". The candidate-list ceiling is measured separately as retrieval failure @50 (Figure 5), and the paper states the principle explicitly: "High performance in extracting the correct lead term is crucial, as it sets the performance ceiling for the entire coding approach."

i4.basis: How much of the note: "In the prompt, the entire text was supplied, using HTML tags to highlight the lead terms within the original text." How many candidates and what evidence per candidate: "From the 50 results retrieved from the vector store query, GPT-4 was prompted to choose the best-matching ICD code. For the decision, GPT was provided with the lead term, textual evidence, and additional context extracted in Step 2." Context-window reasoning is stated: "The complete lists of code descriptions for diagnoses and procedures contain around 2.5 million tokens each, far exceeding the context window size of current generative models." and "when evaluating 50 code candidates, each accompanied by descriptions for the lead term extracted, the token use becomes significant". Model version and decoding are pinned: "This study used GPT-4 (gpt-4 1106-preview)" / "the model's temperature was set to 0". No numeric max-token or truncation policy is given, but the budget the scorer actually sees (full note, top-50 candidates with descriptions) is stated.

i5.basis: Searched Methods (GPT-4 section, Approach, Steps 1-5), Results, and Discussion ('Motivation of Choices', 'Future Research'). A single generative model (gpt-4 1106-preview) is used at every generative step and a single RoBERTa checkpoint for NER; the two are assigned to different tasks, not crossed. Input form IS varied (raw textual evidence vs GPT-4-invented code description as the retrieval query, Figure 5), but only at one fixed capacity, so no interaction is estimable. Varying model capacity is named only as future work: "Another point for future research is to explore the use of locally runnable LLMs".

i6.basis: Evidence shown is guaranteed local to the note being coded: "In the prompt, the entire text was supplied, using HTML tags to highlight the lead terms within the original text." and "Instead of using NER to extract textual evidence, GPT-4 was instructed to complete a template for each lead term which included a field to capture the full textual evidence for the code." Provenance of the retrieved side is also stated: "we converted the official ICD code descriptions into vectors using OpenAI's 'text-embedding-ada-002' model via the Langchain library [21], and stored them in the Chroma vector database." Retrieval is over the official WHO/ICD description set only, never over other patients' text.

i7.basis: "Specifically, in lead term extraction, a prediction was deemed correct if the predicted text span overlapped with the textual evidence." and "Additionally, the accuracy of lead term extraction was also measured using F1-scores calculated for the actual spans, independently of the CodiEsp script." Scoring is against the gold token-level explainability annotations of CodiEsp-X using the organisers' scripts: "The performance of the ICD coding pipeline and its components was evaluated using precision, recall, and F1-score metrics calculated with the CodiEsp scripts [18,22]." This is externally measured span overlap, not a model self-report.

i8.basis: The system does emit structured objects (the Step-2 template with textual-evidence and context fields; the Step-5 code selection), so NA does not apply. Grepped the full text for 'JSON', 'parse', 'malformed', 'unparse', 'schema', 'missing', 'default', 'invalid', 'format' and read Methods Steps 2 and 5, Evaluation, Results and Limitations: no rate of malformed/unparseable/missing-field output is reported anywhere, and no handling policy for such cases is described. Nearest miss, in dataset creation rather than the scored pipeline: "As instructed, GPT-4 typically extracted a single lead term from these multiterm strings. However, in 549 cases (8%), multiple lead terms were extracted" -- a reported instruction-deviation rate with explicit non-coercion ("The researchers manually resolved 325 of these cases to a single lead term, leaving the remaining cases unmapped due to ambiguity"), but it concerns CodiEsp-X-lead annotation quality, not schema compliance of the coding pipeline's output.

i9.basis: Grepped the full text for 'bootstrap', 'permutation', 'McNemar', 'Wilcoxon', 'confidence interval', 'p-value', 'P value', 'P<', 'paired', 'statistic': zero hits (only the reference-list word 'statistical'). The Evaluation section names only precision, recall and F1 via the CodiEsp scripts, with no variance estimate. 'Significant' appears eight times but always colloquially, e.g. "a significant drop in explainability F1-score was observed, falling from 0.509 to 0.378" and "retrieval failures for procedures dropped significantly, from 62 to 30 out of 127" -- no test statistic accompanies either. Note the key contrast (0.305 vs SOTA 0.633) is against literature-quoted numbers, so a paired note-level test would not have been possible for that comparison.

i10.basis: Searched the Evaluation section, Data Availability, Acknowledgments and the table/figure captions. The only reproducibility claims are about model determinism ("To ensure reproducibility, the model's temperature was set to 0") and data/code release ("The datasets generated or analyzed during this study are available in the 'Enhancing ICD coding with LLMs' repository [32]", github.com/putssander/icdllmeval). Nothing states that Tables 1-2 or Figures 4-5 are generated from stored run artifacts or checked against them rather than transcribed by hand.

note: Access: full text, obtained twice (PMC11835781 via WebFetch, and the identical author-accepted PDF from the Hasselt repository, which I converted with pdftotext and grepped line by line — file at /tmp/claude-13462/-arf-home-mkucukkara-morag-icd/8d0c9055-df86-4207-93aa-4a7d8669d2c7/scratchpad/paper3.txt). Sections searched for every item: Introduction, Methods (GPT-4; Dataset CodiEsp; Dataset CodiEsp-X-lead; Approach; Steps 1-5; Evaluation; Ethical Considerations), Results (all subsections, Tables 1-2, Figures 3-5 captions), Discussion (Summary of Main Findings; Motivation of Choices; GPT-4 Parametric Knowledge; Creating CodiEsp-X-Lead; per-step discussions; Method Recap and Evaluation; Limitations; Future Research), Conclusions, Acknowledgments, Data Availability. Only Multimedia Appendix 1 (a DOCX of GPT-4 parametric ICD-10 knowledge) was not opened; it reports the 52%/47% parametric-knowledge probe and is not plausibly the locus of any checklist item scored N. Score profile 4Y/6N/0?/0NA. Where this paper is unusually strong is item 3: the oracle-substitution cascade in the Evaluation section is a textbook stage-wise error attribution, and the retrieval-failure@50 analysis independently isolates the candidate-list ceiling — this is precisely the decomposition the checklist asks for, and it is what lets the authors diagnose their own 0.305 as a retrieval/selection failure rather than an extraction failure. Item 7 is also genuinely strong because CodiEsp-X is one of the few corpora with gold explainability spans, so grounding is measured externally by construction. The N's cluster in the statistical-rigour and engineering-hygiene half of the checklist (items 1, 9, 10) plus the crossed design (5) and schema reporting (8). Two judgement calls flagged for the parent: (a) item 4 scored Y because the paper states the substantive budget — entire note in the prompt, top-50 candidates each with its description — even though it never gives a numeric max-token or truncation policy; a stricter reader could call this "?". (b) item 8 scored N rather than Y despite the reported 8% (549 cases) rate at which GPT-4 violated the one-lead-term-per-string instruction, because that figure describes annotation of the CodiEsp-X-lead training dataset, not schema compliance of the evaluated pipeline's output; a more generous reader could call this Y. Item 1 is a clean N with high confidence: this is a paper about a pipeline whose own numbers fall well below the published supervised SOTA, and no note-blind floor is offered anywhere to calibrate what 0.305 means.

title: Exploring LLM Multi-Agents for ICD Coding
source_url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15363 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.15363; no arXiv HTML rendering exists — /html/2406.15363v1..v3 all return 404, so the PDF was downloaded and converted with pdftotext -layout)
headline_numbers: MIMIC-III top-50 (1,729 test instances, Mullenbach/CAML split): MAC-II with GPT-4 = precision 0.551, recall 0.633, micro-F1 0.589, macro-F1 0.748 (best macro-F1 in Table 1; LLM-codex is higher on micro-F1 at 0.611). MIMIC-III rare: MAC-II GPT-4 micro-F1 0.376, macro-F1 0.715 (vs LLM-codex 0.302/0.279, MSMN 0.173/0.169, CAML 0.083/0.072). MDACE Profee explainability (172 sentence-ICD pairs): MAC-I GPT-4 precision 0.875, recall 0.601, F1 0.712 (vs LLM-codex 0.608/0.861/0.713). Unconstrained setting (no top-50/rare restriction): MAC-II micro-F1 0.347, macro-F1 0.702.

i1.basis: Searched the full baseline list in §4.2 'Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods' (CAML, MSMN, EffectiveCAN, LLM-codex, Zero-shot CoT, CoT-SC, LLM-designed agent), all six result tables (Tables 1-6), §5.4 Ablation Study and Appendix A.1/A.2. Grepped the whole text for 'frequen', 'major', 'constant', 'random', 'prevalence' — no hits. There is no note-blind / most-frequent-K / prevalence predictor anywhere; the weakest comparator is a single-call zero-shot CoT prompt, which the checklist explicitly excludes.

i2.basis: §4.2: 'We evaluated our proposed multi-agent coding method MAC-I and MAC-II against the following baselines: • CAML [19] employs a convolutional attention network that adapts to different segments of the clinical note for each code. • MSMN [41] applies code description synonyms with multi-head attention and outperforms existing methods on the MIMIC-III common task.' Same split is stated in §4.1: 'We use the public MIMIC-III dataset of ICU discharge summaries with expert ICD codes. As in [19], we only keep instances with one or more of the top 50 ICD codes, resulting in 1,729 test instances.' Supervised numbers are quoted from the literature on that benchmark in Table 1 (CAML micro-F1 0.364, MSMN 0.561, EffectiveCAN 0.556, LLM-codex 0.611) and Table 2.

i3.basis: The system does use a candidate list ('External Knowledge: The agents use the candidate codes and their code descriptions as references', Appendix: 'Please only use ICD-9 codes that are listed below: Candidate Codes: ...', Nc=50), so the item applies. I searched §5.4 Ablation Study (Tables 4 and 5), §5.3, §5.5 Applicability, the Discussion and Appendix A.1, and grepped for 'oracle', 'upper bound', 'random', 'error analysis'. Tables 4-5 are plain component ablations (confrontation strategy on/off, external knowledge on/off, agent roles added one at a time) with no oracle/ceiling over the candidate list, no random-selection null, and no stage-wise error attribution. Notably, for the unconstrained experiment in Table 6 the paper never states how the candidate codes are generated, so candidate-generation recall is never separated from selector behaviour.

i4.basis: Appendix A.1 Implementation Details: 'We use GPT4-8k version (Achiam et al., 2023) as the LLM for this study. We access it securely via the Azure OpenAI API with the responsible use requirement. We truncate the EHRs to fit the 8k token limit and sample with a temperature of 0.1. We also set and test the number of candidate codes Nc to 50, which could change for different applications.' This gives context window, truncation policy and the number of candidates carried in the prompt; the note-length range is also given in the Introduction ('in length from less than 500 words to more than 3000 words').

Two models are used (GPT-4 and GPT-4o) and are crossed with prompting/workflow strategy in Tables 1-2, but (a) GPT-4 vs GPT-4o is a model swap of undisclosed and roughly comparable capacity, never framed or analysed as a capacity/size manipulation, and (b) the actual input-context manipulations — external knowledge on/off (Table 4) and the confrontation strategy — are run on GPT-4 only, and Nc is fixed at 50 with no sweep reported. Context amount and model capacity are therefore never crossed and no interaction is estimated or discussed anywhere in the Results or Discussion.

You assign ICD-9 codes to the discharge summary based on the clinical care that the patients received. You cite the discharge summary as evidence when needed.' The only external material injected is code text, not other patients' notes: 'External Knowledge: The agents use the candidate codes and their code descriptions as references to enhance their ICD coding performance' (§3), instantiated in Appendix A.2 as 'Candidate Codes: 401.9 : Unspecified essential hypertension ...'. Professional medical coders annotate a short text span for each ICD code, indicating the rationale for the code assignment. The MDACE Profee datasets are annotated following the professional fee billing rules. We use the sentences that contain the annotated text spans as the evidence for evaluation. The evaluation dataset consists of 172 sentence-ICD pairs.' ACCESS: Full text obtained (arXiv PDF, 2406.15363, ~795 lines of extracted text). It is the complete manuscript in JMIR-style format: Abstract, Introduction, Related Work, Method (five agents; MAC-I and MAC-II workflows), Experiments (§4.1 Dataset and Metrics, §4.2 Baselines), Results (§5.1 top-50, §5.2 rare, §5.3 MDACE Profee, §5.4 Ablation, §5.5 Applicability), Discussion, Limitations, References, and Appendix A (A.1 Implementation Details, A.2 all agent prompts and the candidate-code block). QUOTE FIDELITY CAVEAT: pdftotext mangled the "ti"/"tt" ligatures in this PDF (rendering "multi" as "mul<i", "significantly" as "signiﬁcantly", "attention" as "aEention"). All quotes above are verbatim with those OCR artifacts repaired back to the obvious intended characters; no words were added, removed or reordered.

TALLY: Y on 4 items (2, 4, 6, 7), N on 6 (1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 10), no ?, no NA.

WHERE THIS PAPER IS UNUSUALLY STRONG: item 7. Unlike most LLM-coding papers it does not rest on model-supplied rationales — it evaluates evidence against MDACE's expert-annotated spans (172 sentence-ICD pairs) and reports precision/recall/F1 against fine-tuned systems (Table 3). Item 4 is also well served: the 8k window, the truncation policy, the temperature and Nc=50 are all stated in the appendix, which is more than most comparable papers give.

WHERE IT IS WEAKEST, AND WHY IT MATTERS HERE: items 1, 3 and 9 interact badly. Every headline claim ("significantly outperforms", "significant improvements on all metrics") is an unpaired eyeball comparison of point estimates, several of which are small (MAC-II 0.376 vs MAC-I 0.366 micro-F1 on rare; MAC-II 0.589 vs MAC-I 0.585 on top-50), and Table 4's ablation deltas are 0.008-0.015 micro-F1 — well within what a paired bootstrap on 1,729 notes would likely call noise. Combined with no note-blind floor and no oracle over the 50-code candidate list, the amount of the reported macro-F1 (0.748) attributable to the candidate list itself rather than to the five-agent choreography is not identifiable from the paper. The top-50 setting is the sharpest case: the candidate list is essentially the whole label set, so "external knowledge" there is close to being handed the answer space, and the paper's own ablation shows removing it costs only 0.008 micro-F1 on rare codes.

ONE BORDERLINE CALL WORTH FLAGGING FOR THE AUDIT: item 5. Tables 1 and 2 do report {CoT, CoT-SC, LLM-designed agent, MAC-I, MAC-II} × {GPT-4, GPT-4o}, which is a genuine crossed method×model grid, and a more lenient coder could read that as satisfying the item. I scored N because the checklist requires context and *capacity* to be crossed: GPT-4 vs GPT-4o is a model swap of undisclosed size that the paper never treats as a capacity manipulation, the genuine context manipulations (external knowledge on/off, confrontation on/off) are GPT-4-only in Table 4, Nc is fixed at 50 with no sweep reported despite the phrase "set and test", and no interaction term is estimated or discussed. If the audit wants to record borderline cases separately, this is the one item where a defensible reader could score Y.

Caveats on two of the Y scores, so the parent can downgrade if the rubric is read more strictly:
- i2 (Y) is a literal-criterion pass. PLM-ICD is on the item's named list and was run by the authors on their own benchmark, but it was NOT tuned on this split: they applied MIMIC-IV pre-trained weights zero-shot to a synthetic outpatient dataset (ACI-BENCH). That is a domain-transfer comparison, not a matched-split supervised baseline, so the 0.40 vs 0.60 gap is confounded with distribution shift. If the item is read as requiring a baseline actually fitted/tuned on the same split, this becomes N.

Two borderline calls worth flagging for the audit:
(a) Item 9 is a near-miss rather than a plain absence. The authors DO run a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test between systems, but the paired unit is the three tasks (n=3), not the 300 shared notes - they had 300 note-level paired observations available and did not use them, and they acknowledge 'This lack of significance is likely due to the small number of tasks and limited statistical power.' During inference, the entire documents were processed." (Partial only for ICL/SFT-BioMistral, where the input is 'a report excerpt, corresponding to the context that surrounds it' with the excerpt width never quantified, and '10 random examples' added to the prompt.)

Input form varies (excerpt+mention vs whole document) but capacity is held constant, so nothing is crossed. The paper itself states the gap in Limitations: "Future work can perhaps assess the impact of using LLMs of different sizes."

i6.basis: Evidence is a span of the note being coded, guaranteed by the decoder: "Like GENRE, our model receives a document (with gold mentions) and outputs the document with annotated mention-entity pairs." and "First, it determines the state as either outside an entity ... If outside an entity, then the possible continuation is to resume copying the input document." Datasets are described as "manually annotated with their ICD-10 codes and textual evidence spans", i.e. spans are local to the record; no cross-patient retrieval exists in the system.

i7.basis: The externally-scored CodiEsp-X (end-to-end entity linking, code + evidence span against manual gold annotation) is reported in Table 4 using the official shared-task scorer: "CodiEsp also proposes an end-to-end entity linking task, CodiEsp-X" and "These were computed with the script by Miranda-Escalada et al. (2020)." Nothing is model-self-reported. i8.basis: Compliance is enforced at decode time and stated rather than measured: "Similarly to GENRE (De Cao et al., 2021), we use constrained greedy decoding, to ensure that the model output is always a valid ICD-10 code representation. This is implemented with a prefix tree of all possible outputs, and by forcing the generated tokens to stay within the set of possible continuations for titles of ICD codes." and for InsGenEL: "During inference, we ensure a valid generation using constrained decoding. ... we use a prefix tree to ensure the model generates valid ICD-10 code representations." Caveat: no numeric malformed/unparseable rate is given, and for InsGenEL (which must re-emit the whole document with |code| delimiters) the paper never reports whether every gold mention actually receives an annotation — dropped mentions would be a silent missing-field failure folded into accuracy.

i9.basis: Grep over the entire extracted text for 'signific|bootstrap|p-value|p <|permut|mcnemar|wilcoxon|confidence interval|standard deviation|seed|variance|paired' returns zero hits. Searched §4, §4.1, Tables 1-6, Appendix C (Experimental Details). All results are single point estimates with no error bars, no repeated runs, and no paired comparison between systems.

(2020)" — a metric-computation script, not a statement that tables/numbers are machine-generated from stored artifacts and checked. title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Extract and Translate Medical Information in Doctors' Notes for Health Records and Diagnostic Billing Codes
headline_numbers: Zero-shot diagnostic-code accuracy 3/25 = 12% correct codes (5 models x 5 synthetic notes); only J02.0 (x3), E86.0 (x2), N17.9 (x1 full, x1 partial) ever correct. JSON structure compliance "near 100%" with prompt-only schema, rising to "100% across all models" once Ollama's structured-output constraint was enabled. Note-transcription string similarity ~96% (llama3.2, mistral, phi4) vs 49.5% (deepseek-r1:8b) and 31.9% (gemma3:270m). Few-shot slightly DECREASED code accuracy vs zero-shot; RAG surfaced a few previously unseen codes but reduced diagnosis-extraction accuracy. Corpus: 74,719 ICD-10-CM codes from the CDC .txt file. Models: deepseek-r1:8b, llama3.2, gpt-oss:20b, gemma3:270m/4b, medllama2:7b, meditron:7b, mistral:7b, phi4:14b.
note: This is a master's-thesis-style arXiv preprint (Hartnett, Huang, Hartnett, Hartnett; LaTeXML-generated 14 Jan 2026). I read the complete HTML full text (Sections 1-6 plus Appendices A-C and references) — ~16.6k words — and grepped it exhaustively for each checklist practice. Key context for interpreting the scores: the evaluation set is FIVE fictional physician-authored notes, run against ~5 models under 3 prompting conditions (25 runs per condition), all on an M3 Max MacBook Pro. The authors are explicit that this is a proof-of-concept and say so themselves: "The benchmark dataset serves as a proof-of-concept but is insufficient for statistical significance and requires expansion to include other fields of practice and medical writing styles." No real patient data, MIMIC, or public ICD benchmark was used at all — MIMIC-IV was deliberately declined on privacy grounds — which is why items 1, 2 and 9 have no way to be satisfied in this design and are genuinely absent rather than merely unmentioned. Code and prompts are public at https://github.com/PeterH33/medCodeLLM. Two scores deserve a caveat: item 7 is scored Y on a verbatim-transcription fidelity metric (difflib similarity of the model's original_document field against the source note), which is externally computed and unfakeable, but it is NOT per-code span grounding — no evidence span is tied to any assigned ICD code. Item 5 is scored Y because 3 context conditions were crossed with a model set spanning 270M-20B and the interaction is narrated explicitly, but the design is not a clean factorial: gpt-oss:20b was dropped mid-study and gemma3:270m was swapped for gemma3:4b for the RAG condition, so model identity confounds family with size.

i1.basis: Searched §4.3 (titled "Baseline (Zero-shot) Performance"), §4.7 Summary of Findings, §5 Discussion, and grepped the whole text for majority/most frequent/prevalence/constant/random/trivial predictors. The paper's only "baseline" is its own weakest prompt — "Zero-shot prompting is considered our baseline" — which the checklist explicitly excludes. Comparators are other LLMs (5 open-weight models, plus a passing mention that "top end commercial LLM agents such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are examined for comparison purposes"). No note-blind constant predictor of any kind is reported.

i2.basis: Grepped the full text and the reference list for TF-IDF, SVM, logistic regression, CAML, LAAT, PLM-ICD, MSMN, MultiResCNN, and for any quoted literature numbers on a shared benchmark — zero hits. §2.1 states supervised/fine-tuned routes were deliberately declined ("we originally planned to use SNOMED CT, MIMIC-IV, or ICD-10 datasets for model training or LoRA fine-tuning ... But these datasets were set aside due to privacy and ethical concerns"). The evaluation set is a newly created 5-note synthetic benchmark (§4.1), so no prior system has numbers on this split. All comparisons are LLM-vs-LLM and prompt-vs-prompt.

i3.basis: Searched §3.2.3 (RAG-Enhanced Prompting), §4.5 (RAG-Enhanced Prompting Results), §4.6 (Error Analysis, five subsections) and §5; grepped for oracle, upper bound, ceiling, recall@k, candidate, error attribution. §4.6 gives a qualitative five-category error taxonomy (structured-output, transcription, code hallucination, few-shot overfitting, system-level failures) with no counts apportioned to retrieval vs. selection, and the paper never reports whether the gold ICD code was present in the retrieved FAISS context — which would be the retrieval ceiling. No random-selection null either. This is a plain component ablation, which the item states is insufficient.

i4.basis: Searched §3.2 System Architecture, §3.2.3, §4.1 Benchmark Dataset Description, §5, and Appendices B-C; grepped for context window, token, max_tokens, num_ctx, chunk, top-k, truncat, embedding. The paper reproduces the prompts and all five notes verbatim, but never states any model's context length, any token or chunk size, the number of retrieved ICD chunks per query, or any truncation policy. "Context window" appears only qualitatively ("it frequently saturated the context windows", "loss of context window", "noise to signal issue within the context window") — notable because context saturation is the paper's headline explanation for the RAG result, yet the budget behind it is never quantified.

i5.basis: "Model size constrains task capabilities — Gemma3:270M was unable to process larger RAG-based prompts, while Gemma3:4B handled them successfully." (§4.7 Summary of Findings). The design crosses three input-context conditions (zero-shot §4.3, few-shot §4.4, RAG-enhanced §4.5) against a model set spanning 270M to 20B parameters, each model run under each condition, and the interaction is stated again in §5: "The 7B parameter models struggled to distinguish between the instructions, the doctor's note, and the RAG context."

i6.basis: "employs a RAG-based architecture in which the model retrieves vectorized medical information from plain text files stored on device" (§3.2), with the source named in §3.1.3: "For proof of concept we focus on International Classification of Diseases 10 Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes retrieved from the US CDC" (74,719 codes from the CDC .txt file, indexed via "LangChain FAISS and Retrieval", §4.1). The retrieval corpus is a code lexicon, not patient text, so cross-patient leakage is impossible by construction, and §3.2 states "no protected health information (PHI) or personally identifiable information (PII) were used in this study. Nor was patient medical information."

i7.basis: "To assess the success of this task the LLM outputs were compared using Pythons native difflib library and determining a simple error rate with a score of 1 being a perfect transcription." (§4.3.2). This is an externally computed exact-quote match against a named reference string (the input note) that the model cannot self-report, and it caught real fabrication (§4.4: "Deepseek and gemma3.2 performed quite poorly with only 49.5% and 31.9% string similarity across tests. We noticed Deepseek consistently summarized the doctor's note instead of transcribing it"). Caveat: it measures verbatim reproduction of the whole note, not span-level grounding of any individual ICD code.

i8.basis: "Despite explicit instructions and providing a rigid JSON schema, many models produced malformed JSON or appended notes and conversational text." (§4.6.1), quantified in §4.3.2 and Figure 9 and again in §4.4: "The inclusion of the Ollama structured output system brought JSON structure compliance rate to 100% across all models." Failures are counted as failures rather than coerced — gpt-oss:20b was excluded because it "consistently failed to produce any output with the structured output system enabled", and llama3.2's missing commas and the ‘‘‘json wrapper tags are reported as invalidating responses.

i9.basis: Grepped the entire text for bootstrap, permutation, McNemar, Wilcoxon, paired, t-test, p-value, and confidence interval — no hits in any methodological sense ("significant" appears only colloquially or when citing others' work). §6 Conclusion states the opposite outright: "The benchmark dataset serves as a proof-of-concept but is insufficient for statistical significance and requires expansion to include other fields of practice and medical writing styles." With 5 notes per condition, no paired test is reported anywhere in §4.

i10.basis: Searched §3.2 (which describes a "Logging System which outputs results for repeatability and analysis" and a custom Unix-tee module for dual logging) and §4.1. Raw model outputs are logged to plaintext files and the code is public on GitHub, but the paper states the results were compiled by hand, not machine-generated under provenance checks: "Extraction of diagnoses and application of diagnostic codes are examined and recorded manually to detect any strange or persistent errors that might cause issues in a medical setting." No statement anywhere that tables or figures are regenerated from stored artifacts or checked against them.

title: MKE-Coder: Multi-Axial Knowledge with Evidence Verification in ICD Coding for Chinese EMRs
headline_numbers: MKE-Coder (evidence set) on a private Chinese EMR test set (8,790 EMRs, 33,243-code Chinese medical-insurance ICD): Macro precision 73.34%, recall 71.90%, F1 72.61%; accuracy 74.32%; p@5 92.73%. Re-run baselines on the same split with the same evidence-set input: T5 F1 64.13% / acc 69.58%, JointLAAT F1 34.12%, MSMN F1 30.89% / acc 68.50% / p@5 94.57%, LAAT F1 29.11%. Candidate-generation recall@50 = 96.58/95.43/95.55% (train/dev/test). Simulated coding: novice coders +6.66% accuracy and +26.02% speed vs MSMN assistance; intermediate +3.30% / +33.00%. Human evidence adjudication: ~49% fully supported, ~47% partially supported, 3.84% invalid.
note:
Access: full text of arXiv v1 HTML, converted locally and read in full. Sections searched for every item: Abstract; §1 Introduction (incl. Table 1); §2 Related Works (2.1-2.4, Table 2); §3 Methodology (3.1 Task Definition, 3.2.1-3.2.3, Algorithm 1, 3.3.1-3.3.3, Eqs 1-14); §4 Experiments (4.1 Datasets + Tables 3-4, 4.2 Baselines and Metrics, 4.3 Implementation Details, 4.4, 4.5 + Tables 5-6 + Fig 5, 4.6 Ablation + Tables 7-8, 4.7 Practicality + Figs 6-9); §5 Conclusion; References. I also ran targeted regex sweeps over the whole text for: p-value/t-test/McNemar/Wilcoxon/bootstrap/permutation/confidence interval/paired (zero hits beyond colloquial "significant"); truncation/max length/context window/512/1024/4096 (zero hits); most-frequent/majority/prevalence/constant/random baseline/oracle/upper bound (zero hits); github/code available/reproducible/artifact (zero hits).

IMPORTANT PROVENANCE CAVEAT: this paper has been WITHDRAWN by the authors. The arXiv landing page states "This paper has been withdrawn by Xinxin You" (v4, last revised 10 Mar 2026), reportedly due to data-preprocessing errors affecting result reliability. No PDF is served. I therefore scored against v1, the last version with full text. The headline numbers above should be treated as retracted by the authors, though the reporting-practice scores (what the paper claims to have done) are unaffected.

CAVEAT ON i5 (the one genuinely borderline call): the paper does run a fully crossed 2x5 design — two input-context conditions (discharge summary vs. MKE-Coder evidence set) applied to each of five methods (LAAT, JointLAAT, MSMN, T5, MKE-Coder), with every cell reported in Fig 5(a)/5(b) and the interaction discussed quantitatively (§4.4: "+12.08% F1 and +15.15% accuracy on average"). That literally satisfies "context and model both varied, interaction estimable." However, the second factor is model IDENTITY/ARCHITECTURE, not model SIZE or a parameter-count ladder: the paper never reports parameter counts and never frames the axis as capacity. A stricter reader applying "model size (or capacity)" narrowly would score this N. I scored Y because a genuine factorial exists and the anti-over-N rule applies, but this cell should be flagged as definition-sensitive if the audit tallies it.

Note on i3: the "ceiling" evidence is the candidate-generation recall@N sweep (95%+ at N=50, 98%+ at N=100), which is a true upper bound on what the downstream selector can possibly achieve. It is not labelled "oracle," and there is no random-selection null or stage-wise error attribution (e.g. no "X% of errors were retrieval failures"), so this is the weakest of the Y's.

Note on i8: scored NA because the inference module is a prompt-tuned masked-LM binary classifier — p(y|T)=p([mask]=phi(y)|T) with verbalizer V1="yes", V0="no" — functionally a classifier head over two label words. There is no free-form structured object (JSON, field list) that could be malformed or missing fields, so schema-compliance reporting cannot apply.

Note on i1 vs i7: the paper's human comparisons (advanced coders as gold standard; novice/intermediate coders unaided vs. MSMN-assisted vs. MKE-Coder-assisted) are human baselines and explicitly do NOT satisfy i1 per the checklist rule. They DO satisfy i7, since the evidence-support adjudication is done externally by human coders rather than self-reported by the model.

i1.basis: Searched §4.2 'Baselines and Metrics' (only LAAT, JointLAAT, MSMN, T5 — all read note text), §4.5 Tables 5-6, §4.6 ablation Tables 7-8 (every ablation still reads EMR text: 'w/o evidence retrieve' falls back to discharge summaries), and §4.7 (comparisons are to human coders and to MSMN). Regex sweep over the full text for 'most frequent', 'majority', 'prevalence', 'constant', 'random baseline', 'label prior' returned zero hits. No note-blind constant/K-most-frequent-codes predictor is reported anywhere.

i2.basis: §4.2: 'We choose the following competitive methods as baselines. We measure the results using macro F1, accuracy, and precision@5. LAAT&jointLAAT Vu et al. proposed a label attention model for ICD coding, which can handle both the various lengths and the interdependence of the ICD code-related text fragments [46]. ... MSMN Yuan et al. proposed a multiple synonyms matching network to leverage synonyms for better code representation learning, and finally help the code classification [5]. MSMN is the state-of-the-art method for automatic ICD coding.' These supervised baselines are re-run by the authors on the same Chinese split (Tables 5 and 6: LAAT 29.11% F1, JointLAAT 34.12% F1, MSMN 30.89% F1, T5 64.13% F1 vs MKE-Coder 72.61% F1).

i3.basis: §4.3 Implementation Details: 'During the experiment, we set the number of candidate codes for each diagnosis to 50. Under this setting, the recall rate of both the training set, the development set, and the test set exceeds 95%. If the number is increased to 100, the recall rate can exceed 98%, we chose 50 for efficiency.' Table 3 reports this ceiling per split: 'Recall rate ... 96.58% / 95.43% / 95.55%', captioned as 'the recall rate of the candidate ICD codes to the correct ICD codes for the training set, development set, and test set respectively.' This is an explicit upper bound on what the candidate list makes available to the selector.

i4.basis: §4.1: 'We also show the mean, variance, and median values of the candidate codes of each diagnosis, the evidence of each candidate code, and tokens of each evidence respectively in Table 4.' Table 4 gives: 'Candidate codes per diagnosis 13.17 / 8.6 / 10', 'Reliable evidence per candidate code 3 / 2.4 / 2', 'Tokens per evidence 43.66 / 52 / 7'. Combined with the template of Eq. 11 ('T = [CLS] E'_{d,c_i} [soft][soft][soft] c_i [soft] [mask]'), this states how much evidence per candidate the scorer sees. Caveat: no context window, max-token cap, or truncation policy is stated — regex sweep for 'truncat', 'max length', 'context window', '512/1024/4096' returned zero hits.

i5.basis: §4.4: 'To validate the effectiveness of the evidence set by MKE-Coder for automatic ICD coding, we differentiate whether the discharge summary from the Electronic Medical Record (EMR) or the evidence set generated by the MKE-Coder is used as input, as indicated in parentheses after each method'. Caption of Tables 5/6 and Figure 5: 'For each baseline, use ”discharge summary” and ”evidence set” by MKE-Coder as inputs respectively.' This is a fully crossed 2 (context form) x 5 (LAAT, JointLAAT, MSMN, T5, MKE-Coder) design with every cell reported in Fig 5(a)/(b), and the interaction quantified: 'On average, the methods that use evidence sets as input improve F1 score and accuracy 12.08% and 15.15%, respectively, compared to the methods using discharge summary as input.' See the note field — the second factor is model architecture, not a parameter-count/capacity ladder, so this cell is definition-sensitive.

i6.basis: §1: 'Additionally, we utilize an evidence retrieval module that leverages prior knowledge from ICD coders to locate supporting text descriptions within the EMR for each axis of the candidate code.' §3.2.2 confines retrieval to sections of the record being coded: 'The set of all possible locations where evidence may appear in the medical record, as determined by the prior knowledge table above, is denoted as L_{d,c_i}', with Algorithm 1 taking as Input 'Diagnosis d, Set of candidate codes C_d, Medical Record containing Sections L'. We set three levels: fully supported, partially supported, and unable to be supported (Fig 7 (a)).' With the verbalizer, the probability distribution of Y can be obtained by the probability distribution of V at the [mask] position, which is formalized as follows: p(y|T)=p([mask]=phi(y)|T)' (Eq. 14). This is functionally a classifier head over two label tokens — there is no JSON/field-structured emission that could be malformed, unparseable, or missing fields, so the item cannot apply.

Regex sweep over the full text for 'p-value', 'p <', 't-test', 'McNemar', 'Wilcoxon', 'bootstrap', 'permutation test', 'confidence interval', 'paired' returned zero hits. i10.basis: Searched §4.3 Implementation Details (which reports only learning rate, dropout, weight decay, batch size, fp32, GPU model/memory and wall-clock training hours), all table captions (Tables 1-8), and the Conclusion. Regex sweep over the full text for 'github', 'code available', 'data available', 'reproducib', 'artifact', 'script' returned zero hits.
