title: Large Language Models for Automated ICD-10 Coding of Obstetric Clinical Notes in Portuguese: Comparison With Human Coders
headline_numbers: Best model GPT-4o: micro-F1 0.3675 (95% CI 0.3531-0.3818) at three-character category level and 0.1474 (95% CI 0.1361-0.1589) at leaf level, over 1,117 Brazilian-Portuguese obstetric discharge notes (abstract rounds these to 0.36 and 0.15). Fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini was worst at category level (micro-F1 0.2107). Blinded clinician-validated precision on a 315-note subset: gold standard 0.77 (95% CI 0.74-0.79) vs GPT-4o 0.59 (0.56-0.62), DeepSeek-V3 0.54, GPT-4o-mini 0.43, Sabia-3.1 0.35, Gemini 1.5 Flash 0.32, fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini 0.30; "gold gap" (gold codes rejected by the clinician) = 23%. PT->EN translation changed micro-F1 by +0.0006 (Sabia-3.1), -0.0278 (DeepSeek-V3), -0.0436 (GPT-4o) at category level.

i1.basis: Searched Methods ('Models and Inference' enumerates every system run), all Results sections, Tables 1-5, Discussion, and Supplement S1.2/S2.1/S2.3 (Tables S1-S6). The only comparators are six general-purpose LLMs, one fine-tuned LLM, the human gold standard, and a blinded clinician. No most-frequent-K, majority-class, prevalence or constant note-blind predictor is ever scored. Label prevalence appears only as a descriptive statistic in Table S1 ('Top-10 coverage (3-character categories) 58.30%'), never evaluated as a baseline.

i2.basis: Searched Methods 'Models and Inference' ('We evaluated six general-purpose LLMs plus one specialist variant: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Sabia-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 1.5 Flash, and a fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini'), Tables 2-5, the Discussion comparison paragraph, and Supplement S1.2/S1.3. No TF-IDF, SVM, logistic-regression, CAML/LAAT/PLM-ICD/MSMN/MultiResCNN-class system is re-run or quoted on this corpus. The only supervised system is a fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini, i.e. another LLM (and trained on code-description pairs, not this split). Numbers cited from Dong et al., Soroush et al., and Hou et al. (~0.69 micro-F1) are from different, English benchmarks; the pre-Transformer Portuguese work (ref 17, Reys et al.) is named in the Introduction/Discussion but never run or quoted numerically on these notes.

i3.basis: Searched Methods ('Task Definition and Label Space', 'Prompting and Output Format', 'Human Agreement', 'Statistical Analysis'), all Results, and Supplement S1.5 and S2.3. The system is direct end-to-end LLM generation with no retrieval or candidate-generation stage (the Discussion lists 'retrieval-augmented architectures' as untried future work), and the paper reports no oracle/upper bound over a candidate list, no random-selection null, and no stage-wise error attribution. The 23% 'gold gap' and the union candidate pool used in clinician validation are a human-agreement ceiling and an annotation device, not an isolation of a pipeline stage's ceiling.

i4.basis: Methods, Task Definition: 'We framed coding as multi-label assignment of ICD-10 codes from full, free-text notes.' Supplement S1.1 quantifies what that means: 'The distribution of note lengths is detailed in Figure S1, with notes containing a median of 222 tokens (IQR 178-292) and an average of 251.1 +/- 124.8 tokens.' The verbatim system+user prompts, with the note passed whole as '{clinical_note_text}', are printed in Supplement S1.4, and decoding is specified ('temperature = 0 (deterministic decoding); remaining parameters followed vendor defaults'). No truncation is applied and none is needed. (No explicit context-window or max-output-token figure is given, but the amount of note text the scorer sees is fully stated and quantified.)

i5.basis: Searched Methods ('Models and Inference', 'Portuguese-to-English Translation Condition'), Results Tables 2-4, and Supplement S1.2 and S2.3 (Table S5). The amount of input context is never varied: every model receives the same full note with the same prompt. The only crossed manipulation is input language (native Portuguese vs machine-translated English) x three model identities (GPT-4o, Sabia-3.1, DeepSeek-V3) in Table 4, which varies vendor/model identity rather than size or capacity. The paper's one genuine capacity contrast, GPT-4o vs GPT-4o-mini, is run only in the Portuguese condition, so no context x capacity interaction is estimable. Table S5 varies the translation engine with the coder held fixed (Sabia-3.1), i.e. context one at a time.

i6.basis: The system retrieves nothing and displays no evidence: Methods, Prompting and Output Format, 'For each model, we requested JSON-only outputs listing ICD-10 codes (no explanations)', and the verbatim prompt (Supplement S1.4) instructs 'identify only the ICD-10 codes most relevant to that note, without any explanations or additional information.' There is no retrieval or candidate-evidence stage anywhere in the pipeline (retrieval-augmented architectures are named as future work in the Discussion), so provenance of displayed evidence cannot apply.

i7.basis: Supplement S1.5, Human Validation Protocol: "The reviewer's task was to mark each candidate code as 'appropriate' or 'not appropriate' based on whether there was sufficient evidence within the clinical note to justify its assignment." Corroborated in Methods, Human Agreement: 'the reviewer was blinded to source (gold vs. model and model identity) and instructed to mark each code as clinically appropriate (TRUE) or not appropriate (FALSE) for that note.' This is external, blinded human adjudication of whether the note grounds each emitted code, reported as clinician-validated precision (PPV_H) in Table 5 with Wilson 95% CIs; nothing about it is model self-reported.

i8.basis: Searched Methods 'Prompting and Output Format' and 'Task Definition and Label Space', all Results, and Supplement S1.2 and S2.1. The paper describes the constraint machinery ('we enforced structured output and validated the response schema with Pydantic (v2)'; for DeepSeek-V3 'we instructed JSON in the prompt and then parsed the returned text with conservative tokenization and our ICD-10 regex normalization') but never reports a malformed, unparseable, or missing-field rate, and silently drops bad output: 'Out-of-scope/invalid tokens were discarded prior to scoring.' Table S4's caption promises 'notes (n), notes with >=1 valid prediction (%)', but the published table has only seven columns (Model; predictions per note mean+/-SD; median [IQR]; distinct leaf codes; distinct 3-char categories; top-10 and top-20 coverage) - the validity column is absent (verified by parsing the .docx table XML directly).

i9.basis: Searched Methods 'Statistical Analysis', every Results section, and Supplement S2.2 (Figures S5-S17). Uncertainty is reported only as per-system marginal CIs: 'we computed 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using non-parametric bootstrap resampling. For each metric, we generated 10,000 bootstrap samples by resampling the 1,117 notes with replacement', plus Wilson intervals for the clinician-validated proportions. System comparison is done by inspecting overlap - 'the substantial overlap in their confidence intervals suggests their performance was statistically comparable' - which the checklist explicitly excludes. No paired bootstrap, permutation, McNemar, or Wilcoxon test on matched notes appears anywhere, and no p-value is reported.

i10.basis: Searched Data Availability, Declarations, Methods 'Statistical Analysis', and the whole Supplement. The paper states only that code is public ('This repository includes all code necessary to reproduce the experiments reported in the manuscript, including preprocessing, model inference, evaluation metrics, and visualizations') - a code-availability claim, not a statement that the reported tables/numbers are emitted from stored artifacts and checked. Internal inconsistencies consistent with manual transcription survive into the text: Results give GPT-4o micro-F1 0.37 while the Abstract and Discussion say 0.36; the fine-tuned model is 'micro-F1 = 0.19' in the Fine-tuned specialist section but 0.2107 in Table 2 and '0.21' in the primary-endpoint paragraph; its mean codes/note is 5.69 in the text vs 5.68 in Table S4; Table S5 mixes comma and period decimal separators ('0,2191') and its macro-F1 entries (e.g. 0.2897, 0.3810) are arithmetically inconsistent with the macro precision/recall in the same rows.

note:
Access: full text obtained. Research Square blocks WebFetch (HTTP 403) but the PDF is open via direct curl at https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-8712058/latest.pdf; I also downloaded and parsed the supplementary .docx (Supplement S1.1-S2.3, Tables S1-S6, prompts verbatim). Both were searched section by section, plus targeted greps for baseline/TF-IDF/SVM/CAML/LAAT/PLM-ICD/majority/prevalence/oracle/ceiling/McNemar/permutation/paired/Wilcoxon/context window/max_tokens/truncation/malformed/unparseable/schema/retrieval/provenance/reproduce terms. Nothing was scored N on the strength of the abstract alone.

Design note bearing on the scoring: this is a zero-shot/fine-tuned LLM benchmarking study with no retrieval and no candidate-generation stage, which is why item 6 is NA. Item 7 nonetheless scores Y rather than NA - although the system makes no evidence claim of its own, the paper's central secondary analysis is exactly the externally-measured grounding metric item 7 asks for: a blinded, source-masked, randomized-order clinician adjudication of whether each candidate code has sufficient evidence in the note, applied identically to gold and model codes on 315 notes (Table 5). That analysis is unusually strong for this literature and also yields the paper's most interesting number, the 23% gold gap.

Two borderline calls worth flagging for the audit, both resolved against the paper but arguably:
- Item 4 (scored Y): no context-window or max-token figure is stated, but the paper says whole notes are passed, prints the full prompts, and quantifies note length (median 222 tokens). I read the item's disjunctive "how much of the note" as satisfied.
- Item 5 (scored N): Table 4 IS a fully crossed 3-model x 2-language design and even reports a per-model delta-F1, which is an interaction estimate. It fails the item because the factor crossed with context is model identity across vendors, not size/capacity, and because context amount is never varied at all - the paper's only real capacity contrast (GPT-4o vs GPT-4o-mini) exists at just one context level. A reviewer applying a looser reading of "capacity" could defend Y here.

Item 8's N rests on a verified absence rather than an inference: Table S4's caption advertises a "notes with >=1 valid prediction (%)" column that the published table does not contain. I confirmed this by parsing the .docx table XML rather than relying on flattened text extraction. Combined with "Out-of-scope/invalid tokens were discarded prior to scoring" and the regex-parsed DeepSeek arm, no parse-failure rate is recoverable from the paper.

title: To RAG, or Not to RAG? A Comparative Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for ICD Coding of German Tumor Diagnoses
headline_numbers: Qwen3-Embedding-8B best embedding model: 47.8% exact / 72.1% partial (ICD-10, classifier head); 42.7% exact / 73.5% partial (ICD-O, similarity search). Base Llama 3.3 70B + RAG: 38.0% exact / 80.6% partial (ICD-10), 39.6% exact / 75.0% partial (ICD-O). Best overall = fine-tuned Llama 3.3 70B + RAG: 57.4% exact / 83.5% partial (ICD-10, Table S3). Word2Vec baseline: 18.8% exact / 39.0% partial. Data-quality ceilings estimated at 70% (95% CI 60-79) exact and 89% (95% CI 81-94) partial for ICD-10. n = 2,024 unique German tumor diagnosis descriptions.

i1.basis: Searched Methods ("Overview of RAG pipeline", "Implementation of similarity search", "Large Language Models"), all Results subsections, Discussion, and Supplement Tables S3/S4 which enumerate every evaluated configuration. The complete method list is: similarity search, classifier head, zero-shot, three-shot, RAG(similarity), RAG(classifier) - every one reads the diagnosis text. All 12 occurrences of "baseline" refer to Word2Vec, similarity search, classifier head, or zero-shot LLM performance. The paper reports label prevalence (C44.3 = 8.25%, C43.5 = 4.3% of cases) but never builds a most-frequent-code or constant predictor and never compares against one. The 70%/89% "upper bound" figures are a data-quality ceiling, not a floor.

i2.basis: "The embedding models included larger pre-trained language models, as well as Word2Vec, a simpler neural embedding method. The latter was used as a baseline due to its previously demonstrated strong performance in ICD-10-related semantic retrieval for German clinical text" - and the supervised classifier head was hyperparameter-tuned on the same split: "Training parameters, including the learning rate, batch size, and weight decay, were optimized using the Optuna hyperparameter optimization framework". Both the Word2Vec retrieval baseline and the supervised embedding+classification-head models are run by the authors on the identical 2,024-case test set and reported alongside the LLM/RAG systems in Figures 3, 4, 6 and Tables S3/S4.

i3.basis: "For both ICD-10 and ICD-O coding, the codes retrieved from the embedding models are mostly correct (62.6% / 58.6% exact matches in top-3 predictions of ICD-10 / ICD-O codes, and only 15.9% / 15.4% without any code suggestions that match at least partly). Surprisingly, the LLMs could not translate these suggestions into equally good predictions and pick the correct code from the options presented to them." This is an explicit ceiling over the candidate list (62.6% of top-3 lists contain the exact code) contrasted with what the selector actually produced, rendered as Sankey flows from retrieval-support category to final-answer category (Figure 7). A random-selection null is also present: "Comparing few-shot prompting with random examples against RAG with retrieved examples allowed to distinguish gains from the prompting format itself from gains due to the retrieved information."

i4.basis: "Within the RAG framework, up to three retrieved ICD codes and their corresponding diagnosis descriptions from the ICD-10-GM or ICD-O-3 datasets were retrieved (step 3) and integrated into a structured prompt together with the original medical query (step 4)." Output budget is also stated: "In addition, the maximum number of generated tokens was set to 20." The evidence budget is exactly 3 candidates with one standardized description each, the input unit is a short free-text diagnosis description passed in full (no truncation needed or applied), and the verbatim complete prompt is published in Supplement Tables S6 and S7. Note: no LLM context-window size is named, but the item is satisfied via "how much of the note" and "how much evidence per candidate".

i5.basis: "Base Llama 3.1 8B demonstrated the largest partial-match gains with RAG, highlighting the significance of external evidence for smaller base models. In contrast, the improvement for Llama 3.3 70B was more modest, yet still sufficient to increase ICD-10 partial-match performance to 80.6% and meet the predefined confidence-band criterion." Supplement Tables S3/S4 give the full factorial crossing: 4 context conditions (zero-shot, three-shot random, RAG-similarity-search, RAG-classifier-head) x 4 model configurations (Llama 3.1 8B base, 8B PEFT, Llama 3.3 70B base, 70B PEFT), within one model family so capacity is varied cleanly. The interaction is explicitly estimated and interpreted (context helps the small model more). Embedding capacity is separately crossed with retrieval strategy across nine models spanning ~100M to 8B parameters.

i6.basis: "The retrieval knowledge base was constructed exclusively from standardized Alpha-ID, ICD-10-GM, and ICD-O-3 classifications." Reinforced in the Introduction: "For building the knowledge base of the models, we use only standardized classifications to avoid site-specific bias in the results", and in the pipeline description: "Here, the standardized descriptions for the codes from the ICD-10 and ICD-O classification were used instead of the Alpha-ID and ICD-O-3-LE texts. This choice was made to avoid overly specialized descriptions." Provenance is fully stated and cross-patient contamination is impossible by construction: the knowledge base contains only public code-catalogue entries and no patient text at all.

i7.basis: "For both ICD-10 and ICD-O coding, the codes retrieved from the embedding models are mostly correct (62.6% / 58.6% exact matches in top-3 predictions of ICD-10 / ICD-O codes, and only 15.9% / 15.4% without any code suggestions that match at least partly)." The quality of the displayed evidence is scored externally against the gold code, not self-reported by the model, and Figure 7's flows externally measure whether the model's final answer honoured the evidence it was shown: "A large portion of code suggestions with exact matches were finally answered with a code that matches only partly." No model-supplied rationale or confidence flag is used for this; the only confidence scores reported are classifier-head softmax probabilities (Figure 5), which are also external to the LLM.

i8.basis: "From the Sankey plots, it also becomes clearer that base Llama 3.1 8B exhibited a large portion of malformed outputs in the ICD-O coding task. In all other cases, the rate of malformed outputs was very low and therefore negligible." Figure 7's caption defines the category explicitly: "The right columns show whether the final model answer was an exact match, partial match, mismatch, or could not be parsed (malformed)." Malformed is carried as its own terminal outcome category rather than coerced to a default that would feed ranking, and the Discussion reiterates it: "which was prone to generate malformed or hallucinated outputs".

i9.basis: Searched the full main text and the entire 6-page Supplementary Material for bootstrap, permutation, McNemar, Wilcoxon, paired, p-value, and test statistic - zero hits for all. The Methods "Evaluation metrics" section defines only accuracy, weighted F1 and macro F1, with no inferential procedure. The six "confidence interval" mentions all refer to the 95% CI on the externally estimated data-quality ceiling (70%, 95% CI 60-79%), i.e. a band on an upper bound, not a paired comparison between systems. Supplement Tables S3-S6 report bare point estimates with no CIs or p-values. System differences are asserted descriptively ("exceeded the retrieval baseline by 1.5 percentage points"). The single occurrence of "significance" is colloquial: "highlighting the significance of external evidence for smaller base models".

i10.basis: Searched the Discussion data/code-sharing paragraph, Authors' Contributions, Statements and Declarations, Funding, and the whole Supplementary Material for provenance, transcribed, generated from, data availability, code availability, github, gitlab, zenodo, repository. The paper commits to sharing code and data ("Alongside our code, we also publish the dataset that we created from a combination of the Alpha-ID classification and translation tables to ICD-O" ... "allowing the reproducibility of our methods") and credits evaluation software ("L.O.R contributed to the development of the evaluation software"), but nowhere states that the reported tables/numbers are machine-generated from stored run artifacts or checked against them rather than hand-transcribed. Releasing code is a different claim from table-provenance checking.

note:
ACCESS: Full text obtained. medRxiv serves Cloudflare 403 to both WebFetch and curl, so I retrieved the article through the r.jina.ai text proxy (74 KB, complete: Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusion, Contributions, Declarations, References), plus the Supplementary Material PDF (DC1/media-1.pdf, 6 pages, Tables S1-S7 including the full verbatim prompt templates). Abstract independently confirmed against the biorxiv/medRxiv API and Europe PMC (PPR1246021). Only the Excel supplement (DC2/media-2.xlsx, per-model result grid) was not parsed; its headline contents are duplicated in Tables S3/S4, which I did read.

SCORE SUMMARY: 7 Y, 3 N, 0 ?, 0 NA.

This paper scores unusually well. Its central contribution is essentially item 3: Figure 7's Sankey analysis separates what retrieval made available (62.6% of top-3 candidate lists contain the exact ICD-10 code) from what the LLM selector did with it, and the paper's headline finding is that the selector destroys retrieval headroom rather than that retrieval fails. Item 5 is a genuine full-factorial crossing (4 prompting conditions x 4 LLM configurations within one model family, Tables S3/S4), not the confounded "models with different context lengths" pattern. Item 8 is satisfied unusually cleanly because malformed output is a terminal category in the Sankey rather than a coerced default.

The three N's are real and were checked directly, not inferred from silence:
- i1 (note-blind floor) is the most consequential gap. The test set is skewed dermatological (C44.3 alone = 8.25%), the paper reports that prevalence, and macro F1 trails weighted F1 by ~20-22 points - all of which makes a most-frequent-code floor exactly the comparison a reader wants. It is absent. The paper substitutes a data-quality CEILING (70% exact / 89% partial for ICD-10) which anchors the reader at the top of the scale but leaves the bottom unanchored.
- i9 (paired testing) is absent outright: no test of any kind appears anywhere, yet conclusions rest on margins as small as 1.5 percentage points ("exceeded the retrieval baseline by 1.5 percentage points"). On n=2,024 that margin is well inside sampling noise, and the paper's ICD-O headline claim depends on it.
- i10 (table provenance) is absent; code/data release is promised but is a distinct claim.

Two judgment calls worth flagging for the audit, both resolved toward Y under the "look before you conclude" rule:
- i4: no LLM context-window figure is ever named. I scored Y because the item's alternative criteria are fully met - the input unit is a one-line diagnosis description passed whole with no truncation, the evidence budget is exactly 3 candidates with one standardized description each, and the complete prompt is printed verbatim in Tables S6/S7. A stricter reader wanting an explicit token budget could argue "?".
- i7: the externally measured quantity is the correctness of the retrieved candidate list against gold, plus the flow showing when the model departed from correct evidence it was shown. That is external and non-self-reportable, but it is not span overlap or human adjudication of evidence in the narrow sense. Y is defensible; a narrow reader could argue NA on the grounds that the system displays candidate codes rather than textual evidence spans.

Also of note: the paper declares TRIPOD-LLM compliance ("This study was reported in accordance with the TRIPOD-LLM statement") yet still lacks a note-blind floor and any paired significance testing - a useful data point for the manuscript's argument that existing LLM reporting guidelines do not cover these particular failure modes.

title: Automated ICD-O-3 Coding of Real-World Pathology Reports Using Self-Hosted Large Language Models (Arzideh et al., medRxiv 2025.07.23.25332040; published as JCO Clin Cancer Inform, doi 10.1200/CCI-25-00254)
headline_numbers: ICD-O topography, exact match, with anatomical context: Qwen3-235B-A22B best, micro-F1 71.6% (CI95 70.9-72.3), macro-F1 29.9%. Topography, first-three-characters: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct best, micro-F1 84.6% with context and 87.2% without context; macro-F1 23.8-25.0%. ICD-O morphology: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B best, exact micro-F1 34.7% / macro-F1 6.5%; first-three-characters micro-F1 77.8% / macro-F1 32.3%. Removing anatomical context cost Qwen3 a 44% relative drop (71.6% -> 40.4%) and DeepSeek-70B a 33% relative drop (64.3% -> 42.8%). Small models collapse: DeepSeek-8B exact topography micro-F1 25.4% with context vs 4.3% without; morphology exact micro-F1 0.3%. Corpus: 21,364 reports / 10,823 patients, single German hospital, 80.15% skin (C44). Evaluation restricted to the intersection where all five models produced output: 15,608 topography pairs, 18,118 morphology pairs.
note:
ACCESS ROUTE. doi.org redirected to medrxiv.org, which serves Cloudflare 403 to both WebFetch and curl (also for the .full.pdf and the JATS .source.xml). I retrieved the complete rendered main text through a text-extraction proxy (r.jina.ai) of the v1.full HTML, 58 KB, saved at /tmp/claude-13462/-arf-home-mkucukkara-morag-icd/8d0c9055-df86-4207-93aa-4a7d8669d2c7/scratchpad/jina.txt. That capture contains Abstract, Introduction, Methods (Ethics, Dataset, Prompt Engineering, Models, Evaluation), Results (Dataset characteristics, Processing performance, ICD-O Topography Results, ICD-O Morphology Results, Error Analysis), Discussion incl. limitations paragraph, Declaration of interest, Data Availability, Acknowledgments, and all 44 references. I searched every one of these for each checklist item.

WHAT I COULD NOT SEE. Supplementary Figures 1-6 and Supplementary Tables 1-3 (prompt texts, model overview, sampling parameters, full per-experiment results) are referenced but not in the HTML body and are behind the same Cloudflare block. Figures 1-8 are images; I have only their captions, which are reproduced in full in the capture. I also fetched the published JCO CCI version (10.1200/CCI-25-00254) - the ASCO landing page and the PubMed record (PMID 41812101) - and its structured abstract/Methods summary matches the preprint with no added baseline, no added statistical test, and no code-availability statement, so peer review does not appear to have changed anything relevant to items 1, 2, 9 or 10.

WHERE THE PAPER IS GENUINELY STRONG. Item 8 is the standout and I scored it Y without reservation: the paper devotes an entire Results subsection plus Figure 2 to per-model output-production failure rates (82.2%-91.5%), diagnoses the cause (DeepSeek's <think> reasoning tokens eating the input budget), and then explicitly refuses to coerce or impute - it drops every report that any model failed on, shrinking the evaluation set from 21,364 to 15,608 / 18,118 pairs. This is exactly the discipline item 8 asks for and most LLM-coding papers omit it. Item 5 is also a real Y: the design is a clean 5-model x 2-context crossing on the topography task (every model run with and without the anatomical code list, Figure 3A/B and 3C/D), the capacity arm contains a within-family contrast (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama 70B vs 8B, same distillation data), and the Discussion explicitly reads off the interaction - the drop from removing context is 44% for Qwen3-235B, 33% for DeepSeek-70B, and catastrophic for the 8B (25.4% -> 4.3%), while Llama-3.3 actually improves. Figure 7 adds a second context axis (report length) crossed against all five models.

WHERE I SCORED N AND WHY I AM CONFIDENT. Items 1, 2, 3, 9, 10 are N, not "?", because the full Methods and Results are in hand and the design leaves no room for the practice. Methods lists exactly five artefacts under "Models" - all five are LLMs - and the Evaluation subsection defines the entire measurement apparatus in one paragraph (micro/macro P/R/F1, exact vs first-three-character matching, bootstrap CIs). There is no sixth row anywhere. On item 1, the paper repeatedly analyses performance as a function of code frequency (Figures 5 and 6, top-five most frequent codes) and notes 80.15% of the corpus is C44, which makes the absence of a most-frequent-code floor conspicuous: with that class skew a constant "always emit C44 + 809" predictor would score non-trivially on the micro-averaged headline numbers, and nothing in the paper bounds that. On item 2, the Introduction cites Rios et al. 2021 (neural multi-task ICD-O-3 coding) and Qiu et al. 2018 (deep learning for primary sites) as motivation, so the authors are aware of the supervised literature, but neither is re-run nor quoted as a comparison, and the corpus is a private single-institution German set with no public benchmark counterpart. The Discussion's comparisons (Truhn, Huang, Soroush) are all LLM-vs-LLM on different data. On item 3 the with/without-context contrast is a prompt ablation, and the "Error Analysis" section is per-class and per-length stratification, not stage attribution; there is no candidate-generation stage, no oracle over the supplied code list, and no random-selection null. On item 9 the paper reports 1,000-iteration bootstrap CIs on each model's own score - the exact construct the checklist names as not counting - and the CIs are used informally to rank models; nowhere is a paired difference tested, despite the common-subset restriction having set up the pairing perfectly. On item 10 the Data Availability Statement covers data only, there is no code-availability statement, no repository, and no claim about how tables were produced.

ITEMS 6 AND 7 ARE NA, AND THIS IS A DESIGN FACT NOT AN OMISSION. The system retrieves nothing per-note: the only "context" is a static ICD-O-3 topography code list pasted into prompt 1, whose provenance is stated (WHO/IARC ICD-O-3 and the German BfArM classification, refs 34-35) and which is by construction not another patient's text. It displays nothing: "all models were prompted to return only the codes without any explanations." So there is no evidence artefact for item 6 to trace or item 7 to score externally. Qwen3 thinking mode was enabled and DeepSeek emits <think> blocks, but the paper treats that trace purely as a token-budget cost, never as evidence, and never evaluates it - so no evidence claim is made and item 7 cannot bite. If a scorer preferred N over NA on item 6 the argument would be that the code-list provenance is stated and therefore the item is satisfiable as Y rather than NA; either way it is not a failure.

ITEM 4 IS THE ONE JUDGEMENT CALL. I scored Y. The main text states that whole reports are the input, that there is no truncation, that over-length reports simply fail and are excluded (which is what produces the 82.2%-91.5% extraction rates), that reasoning tokens shrink the usable input window, and it names one concrete window (gemma-3, 128k). Report lengths are quantified throughout (the Figure 7/8 length bins run 800 to 5,200 characters, with a tail past 12,800). The limitations paragraph owns the resulting bias: "excluding reports due to context token-length constraints may have biased the dataset against more complex cases." What is NOT in the accessible text is a per-model context window or max_tokens table - Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 are said to hold model architecture and sampling parameters, and I could not open them. A stricter scorer wanting an explicit per-model token number could reasonably mark this "?"; I judged the stated policy (full note, no truncation, exclude on overflow, with the bias acknowledged) to be a substantive answer to "how much text does the model actually see."

OVERALL SHAPE. 3 Y, 5 N, 2 NA. The paper is unusually honest about the two things LLM-coding papers most often hide - output-production failure rates and the input-budget bias they create - and it has a genuinely crossed context x capacity design. What it lacks is any floor or ceiling: no trivial predictor beneath it and no supervised baseline beside it, on a corpus that is 80% one topography group, which means the headline micro-F1 figures are uninterpretable as evidence of note-reading. The authors' own conclusion ("not yet sufficient for fully automated, unsupervised use") is appropriately cautious, but it is reached by comparing LLMs with each other rather than against anything that would calibrate the numbers.

i1.basis: Searched Methods (Models subsection lists exactly five artefacts, all LLMs; Evaluation subsection defines the whole metric apparatus), all five Results subsections including Error Analysis, all Figure 2-8 captions, and the Discussion. No constant, most-frequent-code, majority-class or label-prevalence predictor appears anywhere. Notable given the paper's own report that C44 is 80.15% of topography codes and 809 is 33.90% of morphology codes, which a note-blind predictor would exploit.

i2.basis: Searched Methods (Models, Evaluation), Results, Discussion and all 44 references. Only five LLMs are run. Rios et al. 2021 (neural multi-task ICD-O-3 coding, ref 4) and Qiu et al. 2018 (deep learning for primary sites, ref 5) are cited in the Introduction as motivation but neither is re-run nor quoted as a same-benchmark comparison; the corpus is a private single-institution German set. The Discussion's comparisons (Truhn, Huang, Soroush) are LLM-vs-LLM on different data. Confirmed no baseline in the published JCO CCI abstract either.

i3.basis: Searched Methods (Prompt Engineering) and Results (Processing performance, Error Analysis). The with/without-anatomical-context contrast is a prompt ablation, and Error Analysis stratifies by code frequency (Fig 5, 6) and report length (Fig 7, 8) rather than attributing errors to stages. There is no candidate-generation or retrieval stage, no oracle/upper bound over the supplied ICD-O-T code list, no random-selection null, and no stage-wise error attribution.

i4.basis: "All pathology reports served as input for LLM extraction of ICD-OT and ICD-OM codes. However, extraction success varied across models due to context length limitations and differences in output generation patterns. Some models, such as Deepseek, generate reasoning content within “<think>” HTML tags (see Supplementary Figure 4 for an example), which consumes output tokens and thereby reduces the available input context for processing reports." Reinforced by "lightweight multimodal models that can process large contexts up to 128k tokens" (gemma-3) and by the limitation "Furthermore, excluding reports due to context token-length constraints may have biased the dataset against more complex cases." Whole note in, no truncation, overflow excluded rather than clipped. Caveat: per-model context windows / max_tokens sit in Supplementary Tables 1-2, which I could not access.

i5.basis: "In the second prompt, no additional information about the anatomical locations was provided. The rest of the prompt was identical. This way, the impact of the additional context was evaluated to give insights into the performance differences when providing additional context." Fully crossed with five models spanning 8B/12B/70B/235B-A22B (Fig 3A/B vs 3C/D run every model under both context conditions), and the interaction is read off explicitly: "The Qwen3-235B-A22B model experienced a 44% relative performance drop (from 71.6% to 40.4% micro-average F1-score), while DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B showed a 33% relative decrease (from 64.3% to 42.8% micro-average F1-score) when the anatomical meaning of ICD codes was not explicitly provided." A within-family capacity contrast exists (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama 70B vs 8B, "trained on the same dataset as the larger model"), and the 8B falls 25.4% -> 4.3% under the same context removal, so capacity x context is estimable rather than confounded.

i6.basis: The system retrieves nothing per note and displays no evidence: "To make it easier to evaluate the outputs, all models were prompted to return only the codes without any explanations." The only added context is a static ICD-O-3 topography code list in prompt 1, whose provenance is stated (WHO/IARC ICD-O-3 and German BfArM, refs 34-35) and which is by construction not another patient's text. Ground-truth codes were stripped from each report before input ("These codes were extracted to form a ground truth and removed from the report so that the model can generate codes without having the correct answer in the input"). No retrieved or displayed evidence exists for the item to apply to.

i7.basis: The system makes no evidence claim: "all models were prompted to return only the codes without any explanations." Qwen3 thinking mode was enabled and DeepSeek emits <think> blocks, but the paper treats those traces solely as a token-budget cost in the Processing performance subsection and never scores, adjudicates or reports them as justification. Searched Methods (Prompt Engineering, Evaluation), Results and Discussion for any span-overlap, quote-match or human-adjudication metric; none exists because no evidence is produced.

i8.basis: "From the initial 21,364 reports, Llama-3.3 could extract 19,554 ICD-OT codes (91.5%, Fig. 2A). Qwen-3 and Gemma-3 achieved similar results with 19,546 (91.5%) and 19,127 (89.5%) extracted ICD-OT codes. In comparison, the Deepseek models only extracted 18,150 (85%) for the 70B and 17,566 (82.2%) for the 8B variant." And on non-coercion: "To ensure fair comparison across models, evaluation was restricted to ICD-O and report pairs where all models generated predictions... Only reports for which every model generated an ICD-O code prediction were included in the analysis, yielding 15,608 pairs for the ICD-OT task and 18,118 pairs for the ICD-OM task." Failures are counted, attributed to a cause, and dropped rather than defaulted into the ranking.

i9.basis: Searched Methods (Evaluation), every Results subsection, and the Discussion. headline_numbers: 120-note outpatient test set (207 annotated notes: 67 train / 20 dev / 120 test) built on ACI-Bench. Best off-the-shelf Exact Match F1 = 43.0 (Sonnet-3.5v2, simple prompt); PLM-ICD baseline = 24.8. The paper is unusually strong on pipeline decomposition (item 3): it reports an explicit oracle over the expanded candidate list in both Table 5 and Table 8, and footnote 3 correctly explains why the oracle is below 100% (expansion seeds are model-predicted, so gold codes outside the expanded branch are unrecoverable). It is also genuinely crossed on context x capacity (item 5) - Tables 6, 7 and 8 are complete factorial grids over models x prompt/expansion conditions, and the authors state the interaction in words in both §5.2 and Appendix B.3.

Two "Y" calls are borderline and I flag them so the audit can recalibrate:
- Item 4: the candidate-side budget is stated quantitatively and per-candidate rendering is ablated, and the full generation prompt is reproduced, but the paper never states a context window, max-token limit, truncation policy, decoding parameters, or note-length statistics (zero grep hits for any of those terms). There is no experimental-setup subsection and no fine-tuning hyperparameters. A stricter reading of "budget STATED" would score this N.
- Item 7: the external check is expert double-annotation with arbitration of code validity, and verification accuracy is measured against it - so the model's supportedness decision is not self-reported. But there are no evidence spans, no quote-match metric, and no inter-annotator agreement statistic. A stricter reading requiring span/quote-level grounding would score this NA or N.

Item 2 is a clear Y but worth noting: PLM-ICD is applied as a transfer baseline (trained on inpatient MIMIC-IV, evaluated on the outpatient benchmark) rather than retrained on the 67-example train split, which the authors themselves treat as the explanation for its low 24.8 F1. It is nonetheless a named supervised ICD baseline re-run by the authors on the same split, which is what the item asks for.

The four "N"s cluster on statistical and engineering hygiene: no note-blind floor, no parse/schema-failure reporting despite a JSON-mandating prompt, no paired significance test on a 120-note test set where several headline gaps are a few F1 points (e.g. fine-tuned Haiku-3 56.9 -> 57.6 with verification; Sonnet-3.5v1 55.6 -> 55.5, a decrease), and no table-provenance statement.

title: Assessing Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model Performance in Emergency Department ICD-10-CM Coding Compared to Human Coders
source_url: https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.10.15.24315526v1.full (medRxiv is Cloudflare-blocked; obtained via Wayback snapshots https://web.archive.org/web/20241121093206id_/https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.10.15.24315526v1.full.txt and .../20241121093213id_/....full.pdf . headline_numbers: n=500 ED visits (Mount Sinai, Jan–Apr 2024); RAG corpus = 1,038,066 prior ED visits, 10,876 unique codes; 9 LLMs. Valid-ICD-code rate zero-shot 42.4% (Qwen-2-7B) to 95% (GPT-4), rising to ~99.8–100% with the RAG prompt. Human panel (200 discrepant cases, 4 physicians): GPT-4 preferred for accuracy 447 vs 277 (p<0.001) and for specificity 509 vs 181 (p<0.001). LLM judges: GPT-4 260 vs 84 (accuracy, Llama-3.1-70B judge); Llama-3.1-70B 218 vs 90 (Qwen-2-72B judge). Fleiss' kappa: LLM judges 0.595 accuracy / 0.688 specificity; human reviewers 0.307 / 0.346. The paper states retrieval provenance completely and enumerates exactly what reaches the scorer (code description + code + 2021-2023 assignment frequency), which structurally rules out another patient's free text appearing. title: Augmenting Structured Diagnoses through Effective Use of Pre-trained Large Language Models on Clinical Notes

title: Extracting International Classification of Diseases Codes from Clinical Documentation Using Large Language Models (Simmons et al., Applied Clinical Informatics 2025;16:337–344; doi 10.1055/a-2491-3872)
headline_numbers: 50 AHIMA VLab deidentified inpatient notes (23 H&P, 27 progress notes); certified human coder extracted 165 unique ICD-10-CM codes (inter-coder kappa 0.86 on a 20% subset). Primary diagnosis only: Claude 3 26% agreement, kappa 0.25 (category-level: Claude 2.1/Claude 3 36%, kappa 0.35). LLMs emitted 221 (Gemini) to 658 (Llama 2-70b) unique codes vs 165 for the human coder.

title: Evaluating Enhanced LLMs for Precise Mental Health Diagnosis from Clinical Notes

This is a short evaluation preprint, not a systems paper, and the reporting surface is correspondingly thin. Notable: the entire comparator set is three commercial/open LLMs against each other under two prompt configurations. The word "baseline" appears exactly once (line 97, "the baseline coding performance of various LLMs") and refers to the LLMs' own un-augmented performance, not to any external comparator.

Two items deserve explanation of the judgement call:

- i5: Table 1 is structurally a 3-model x 2-configuration grid, which is the closest any item comes to being satisfied. I scored N because the second axis is vendor/model identity, not capacity: GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Flash parameter counts are undisclosed and never stated, and the paper never says which LLaMA 3.2 variant was used - §II.C describes the family as "1 billion and 3 billion parameters ... as well as vision models with 11 billion and 90 billion", while the Introduction says "LLaMa-70b Chat", a size that is not in the LLaMA 3.2 family at all. With capacity undefined and internally contradictory, the context x capacity interaction is not estimable, which is exactly the confound the item excludes. The paper does make an informal interaction remark (LLaMA showed "minimal benefit from the additional context provided by RAG" whereas Gemini "exhibited noticeable improvement"), but never quantifies or tests it.

- i7: scored NA rather than N. The models emit ICD-10 code sets only; they are never asked for rationales, spans, or supporting quotes, and no evidence is displayed to any reader. The "Human Evaluation" section is genuine external expert review (two UIC psychiatry medical coders are acknowledged), but it adjudicates code correctness, not evidence, so there is no evidence claim for a grounding metric to attach to.

Reliability caveats worth flagging to the parent: the Results text contains a verbatim copy-paste error - the sentence "The model also reduced its number of completely different outputs to 13, highlighting its effectiveness in leveraging additional context" appears in both the GPT-4o RAG paragraph and again at the end of the LLaMA RAG paragraph, where 13 is wrong (LLaMA had 41). Gemini is the only model that improves. The Introduction names "GPT-4" and "LLaMa-70b Chat" while the Methods use GPT-4o and Llama3.2, and "Google" is used interchangeably with "Gemini-1.5-Flash" throughout the Results. These inconsistencies are themselves corroborating evidence for the i10 "N" - the tables and prose were clearly assembled and narrated by hand rather than emitted from checked artifacts.

title: Can GPT-3.5 generate and code discharge summaries?
source_url: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11413433/ (also arXiv:2401.13512v2 PDF, 24 pp., which contains Supplementary Materials 1-4)
headline_numbers: GPT-3.5 coding real MIMIC-IV test notes: P 9.46 / R 33.51 / micro-F1 14.76 (set-based hier. F1 17.13; CoPHE 16.72). Every comparator is a trained system (CAML, LAAT, Multi-Res CNN, GPT-3.5); 'baseline' in this paper denotes the non-augmented training set, not a predictor. title: Gold-standard-guided direct preference optimisation for ICD-10-AM and ACHI code assignment from discharge summaries
source_url: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12911-026-03631-w (full text read from the accepted-manuscript PDF: https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1186/s12911-026-03631-w_reference.pdf; supplement: 12911_2026_3631_MOESM1_ESM.pdf)
headline_numbers: DPO-aligned full-parameter Llama-3-8B is the best variant: micro-F1 0.7397 (mapped MIMIC-III, n=1,254, |L|=95) and 0.7834 (SWSLHD Australian hospital, n=5,001, |L|=100); macro-F1 0.6978 / 0.7910; Jaccard 0.5870 / 0.6439. Full fine-tuning without DPO: micro-F1 0.6569 / 0.7078. QLoRA 4-bit: micro-F1 0.5109 / 0.4406. All metrics are restricted to top-50 ICD-10-AM diagnosis + top-50 ACHI procedure codes and to discharge summaries of at most 1,000 words (74.6% of mapped test records and 52.1% of SWSLHD test records were excluded as too long).
note:
Access: full text of the "Article in Press" accepted manuscript (unedited version). Sections searched for every item: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 2 Related Work; 3 Methodology (3.1 SFT / task formulation, 3.2 LoRA-QLoRA baseline, 3.3 DPO incl. 3.3.1 preference-pair construction and 3.3.2 objective); 4 Experimental Setup (datasets, 4.1 code-mapping pipeline, 4.2 model training, 4.3 evaluation metrics); 5 Results and discussion (Tables 7-9, error-type analysis); 6 Limitations; 7 Future Research Directions; 8 Conclusion; Declarations; and Additional file 1 (which contains only code-frequency figures S1-S4).

Design summary: single-stage generative coding — a discharge summary is fed to a fine-tuned Llama-3-8B, which emits a formatted code list. There is no retrieval or candidate generation at coding time (the sentence-transformer top-k=3 retrieval is used only offline to build the ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-AM/ACHI label mapping dictionary, reviewed by one expert coder), and the model produces no rationales, spans, or confidence scores. Hence items 6 and 7 are NA rather than N.

The paper is unusually candid about its own gaps, which makes several N codes explicit rather than inferred: §2 states prior architectures "were not re-implemented or evaluated on the same ICD-10-AM/ACHI label space and data splits"; §6 says future work "should include repeated runs with different random seeds and direct comparison with established automated coding baselines under the same ICD-10-AM/ACHI label space and data splits"; §5/§6 state that observed differences "should be interpreted as descriptive comparisons ... rather than statistically confirmed superiority."

Item 8 deserves a note: the paper repeatedly acknowledges that malformed output occurs ("repeated text, invalid outputs, or failure to generate a usable code list") and describes post-processing ("normalising formatting, removing duplicates, and retaining only codes within the evaluation scope"), but it never reports the RATE of malformed/unparseable output, and it explicitly holds those failures out of the only error analysis it does report. The 3,687/4,941 and 5,443/10,444 exclusions are by word count, not by observed malformation, so they are not a schema-compliance rate.

Item 9 near-miss: the paper does report 1,000-iteration non-parametric bootstrap 95% CIs over test records for every metric of every system — the resample count is stated — but these are per-system CIs, not a paired test on the same notes, which the checklist explicitly excludes.

i1.basis: Searched §4 Experimental Setup, §4.3 Evaluation Metrics, §5 Results (Tables 7, 8, 9) and §6 Limitations: the only comparators are three Llama-3-8B variants (QLoRA 4-bit, full-parameter FT, full FT + DPO). No constant/most-frequent-code/label-prevalence predictor is reported anywhere, despite the label space being explicitly the top-50 most frequent codes.

i2.basis: Searched §2 Related Work and §5/§6. §2 states verbatim: 'These prior models provide important context for automated clinical coding; however, they were not re-implemented or evaluated on the same ICD-10-AM/ACHI label space and data splits in this study. Therefore, they are discussed as related work rather than direct experimental baselines.' No TF-IDF/SVM/CAML/LAAT/PLM-ICD number is quoted on the same benchmark; §6 lists such comparison as future work. The QLoRA 'baseline' is another variant of the same LLM.

i3.basis: Searched §3 Methodology (all subsections), §4.1 mapping pipeline, and §5 Results including the 'Error-type analysis' paragraph and Table 9. The system has no retrieval or candidate-generation stage to decompose; no oracle/upper bound over a candidate list, no random-selection null, and no stage-wise error attribution is reported. Table 9 counts extra-code and missed-code errors of the final output only ('This analysis was limited to code-level set errors'), which is outcome accounting, not a ceiling isolation. §5 also states 'we did not perform a controlled matched-subset ablation to isolate the effect of mapping or dataset source.'

i4.basis: "Results are reported for discharge summaries up to 1000 words; longer notes led to generation failures (repetition or invalid output) in preliminary testing. Importantly, we did not truncate discharge summaries; longer notes were excluded from the reported evaluation." (§5). Also §5: "the quantitative results reported in the following performance tables are limited to discharge summaries within the 1,000-word evaluation setting. Longer summaries were excluded from the reported evaluation rather than truncated." The input is the whole note prompt: "the input prompt consists of an instruction and the discharge summary" (§3.1.1). Note: an explicit context-window/max-token figure is never given, and §4.2 reports only GPU hardware, no sequence-length or other hyperparameters.

i5.basis: Searched §3.2 (QLoRA vs full FT), §4.2 Model Training, §5 Results (Tables 7-8) and §7 Future Directions. Capacity is varied only as full-parameter vs 4-bit-quantised LoRA adaptation of the same Meta-Llama-3-8B backbone; the input context is held fixed (whole note, evaluation restricted to <=1,000 words for every variant), so no crossed context x capacity design exists and no interaction is estimable. §7 explicitly defers this: 'Larger-capacity models (e.g., LLaMA 3 70B) may also be explored' and 'Future work should explore long-context models, section-aware chunking, retrieval-augmented generation'.

i6.basis: The coding system retrieves and displays no evidence: §3.1.1 formulates the task as instruction-following generation from the discharge summary alone, and §7 lists retrieval-augmented generation as future work ('retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to ground predictions in coding standards and code definitions'). The only retrieval in the paper is offline label-mapping over code descriptions (§4.1, sentence-transformer top-k=3 over ICD-10-AM/ACHI Eleventh Edition descriptions), and the Streamlit interface displays only the model's own codes vs the gold code list for the note being reviewed, not retrieved text.

i7.basis: The model emits only code lists; it makes no evidence, rationale, span, or 'supported' claim anywhere. Searched §3.1.1 output template ('ICD-10-AM Diagnosis Codes are: ... ACHI Procedure Codes are: ...'), §3.3.1 preference-record format (query/chosen/rejected fields only), and §4.3 Evaluation Metrics, which reports only set-overlap metrics (micro/macro P, R, F1, Jaccard).

i8.basis: Searched §3.1.1 (post-processing), §5 Results, Table 9 and §6 Limitations. Malformed output is acknowledged but never quantified: '§5: Long-document generation failures, such as repeated text, invalid outputs, or failure to produce a usable code list, were considered separately and were not included in the error-type counts' — and no such separate count is given anywhere in the paper or supplement. §6 repeats the qualitative claim without a rate. Post-processing ('normalising formatting, removing duplicates, and retaining only codes within the evaluation scope') is described with no unparseable/missing-field statistics.

i9.basis: Searched §4.3 ('Confidence intervals' paragraph), Tables 7-8 notes, and §6. The paper reports only per-system percentile bootstrap CIs — 'we sampled test records with replacement for 1,000 bootstrap iterations and recomputed micro-precision, micro-recall, micro-F1...' — which the checklist excludes as not a paired test. No McNemar/permutation/Wilcoxon/paired-bootstrap contrast between systems on the same notes is reported, and §6 concedes: 'the observed differences should be interpreted as descriptive comparisons among the evaluated Llama 3 variants rather than statistically confirmed superiority.'

i10.basis: Searched §4.2, §4.3, §5, the notes under Tables 1-9, §6 Limitations and the Declarations (Availability of data and materials, Authors' Contributions). No statement that result tables or numbers are generated from stored artifacts or checked for provenance; no analysis code/repository is released (only data-access statements). The nearest relevant text concerns annotation provenance, not results: '§3.3.1: All annotations and metadata were stored in a SQLite database (record identifier, dataset source, query/prompt, predicted output, gold-standard output, and timestamp) to ensure traceability.'

title: Evidence-Grounded LLM Validation of MIMIC-IV ICD Labels
headline_numbers: The accessible abstract reports no numeric accuracy figures. It states only the scale and design: 10,000 MIMIC-IV notes processed; two derived label sets (Evidence-Verified, Evidence-Replaced); six replicated ICD coding models (PLM-ICD, LAAT, MultiResCNN, CAML, Bi-GRU, CNN); micro-precision/recall/F1 evaluated with paired bootstrap resampling; qualitative claim that "removing unsupported charted codes from MIMIC substantially improves model performance." Article is Stud Health Technol Inform 2026;336:994-998 (5 pages), PMID 42175002.
note:
ACCESS ATTEMPTS (all failed to yield full text): doi.org/10.3233/shti260328 -> ebooks.iospress.nl/doi/10.3233/SHTI260328 (landing page, abstract only, "Download PDF" button has no resolvable href); ebooks.iospress.nl/pdf/doi/10.3233/SHTI260328 (returns landing HTML, not PDF); /doi/pdf/, /doi/full/, /pdf/10.3233/SHTI260328, /pdf/78622, /pdf/volumearticle/78622 (all HTTP 404); /Download/Pdf?id=78622 ("requested download either does not exist... or access is not allowed"); content.iospress.com (301 -> journals.sagepub.com, IOS Press now on Sage; journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3233/SHTI260328 = 404); r.jina.ai proxy of both the DOI landing page and /volumearticle/78622 (abstract only); PubMed 42175002 (abstract, only full-text link is the IOS DOI); Europe PMC MED/42175002 (no content); PMC search (no matching record); scholar.archive.org (no results); CORE (403); Bing filetype:pdf (nothing); arXiv API author search "Abu Dayeh" (0 results); OpenAlex and Unpaywall both report is_oa true / CC-BY-NC published version but pdf_url = null; Semantic Scholar openAccessPdf points back to the DOI landing page. I located the article's internal volume-article id (78622) via the MIE 2026 volume listing page 10, but the platform's PDF download endpoint refused it.

CONSEQUENCE FOR SCORING: because only the abstract was reachable, seven of ten items are coded "?" rather than "N". Per the audit's own rule, absence of mention in an abstract is not absence of practice — and this is a 5-page MIE conference paper whose methods section I never saw. In particular items 1 (note-blind floor), 3 (pipeline decomposition), 4 (input budget), 5 (crossed context x capacity), 7 (externally measured grounding metric), 8 (schema compliance) and 10 (machine-generated tables) are all plausibly addressed in the unseen Methods/Results without appearing in a ~200-word abstract. Item 7 is the one I most regret not resolving: the paper's central claim is evidence-grounded validation, and whether the extracted quotes were checked against the note externally (exact-string match) or adjudicated by a human is exactly the kind of detail that lives in the Methods, so a "?" here should not be read as a negative.

Note also that this paper's system design differs from a retrieval-augmented coder: it validates pre-existing charted (note, code) pairs rather than retrieving candidates, so item 3's "candidate generation ceiling" framing maps awkwardly onto it, and item 6 is satisfied trivially-by-construction (the evidence is quoted out of the same note being validated).

i1.basis: Searched the full abstract (IOS Press landing page, PubMed record, r.jina.ai render) for any constant/trivial/most-frequent-K/label-prevalence baseline. The abstract names only six supervised coding models; it says nothing either way about a note-blind floor. Methods/Results were unreachable, so this cannot be resolved.

i2.basis: "We replicate six state-of-the-art ICD coding models (PLM-ICD, LAAT, MultiResCNN, CAML, Bi-GRU, CNN) under identical settings as Edin et al. and evaluate micro-precision, recall, and F1 using paired bootstrap resampling."

i3.basis: Looked in the abstract for an oracle/upper bound over a candidate list, a random-selection null, or stage-wise error attribution. The abstract describes a per-(note, code) validation workflow with three steps but reports no ceiling analysis or error decomposition; the Methods/Results, where such an analysis would appear, were inaccessible.

i4.basis: Searched the abstract for context window, max tokens, truncation policy, or how much of the discharge summary the LLM sees. The abstract does not even name the LLM used, so the input budget cannot be determined; this detail would sit in the unreachable Methods.

i5.basis: Looked in the abstract for a crossed design varying input context and model capacity. The abstract refers to "an LLM-based evidence-validation workflow" without naming or enumerating models or context conditions, so it is silent on whether any capacity or context factor was varied, let alone crossed. Not determinable from the abstract.

i6.basis: "We present an LLM-based evidence-validation workflow that examines each (note, code) pair and: (1) determines whether the code is supported by the note, (2) extracts the corresponding evidence quote(s) from the note" — evidence provenance is stated to be the note being coded itself, with no cross-note or cross-patient retrieval in the pipeline.

i7.basis: Searched the abstract for span overlap against gold annotations, exact-quote matching against the source note, or human adjudication of the extracted evidence. The abstract states that evidence quotes are extracted but reports no external verification metric; whether one exists is exactly the kind of Methods/Results detail I could not access.

i8.basis: The workflow plainly emits a structured object (support decision, evidence quote(s), optional replacement code), so NA does not apply, but the abstract reports nothing about malformed/unparseable output rates or default-coercion of missing fields. Unreachable Methods.

i9.basis: "...evaluate micro-precision, recall, and F1 using paired bootstrap resampling." (Caveat: the number of bootstrap resamples is not stated in the accessible abstract; it may be given in the unreachable Methods.)

i10.basis: Searched the abstract for any statement that tables/numbers are generated from stored artifacts or checked for provenance rather than hand-transcribed. Abstracts essentially never carry this statement, and the Methods/Results and any data-availability statement were inaccessible.

title: An automated information extraction model for unstructured discharge letters using large language models and GPT-4 (Siepmann, Baldini, Schmidt, Truhn, Müller-Franzes, Dada, Kleesiek, Nensa, Hosch; Healthcare Analytics 7 (2025) 100378)
source_url: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.health.2024.100378 (full text obtained as the published Elsevier VOR PDF via the University of Duisburg-Essen repository: https://duepublico2.uni-due.de/servlets/MCRFileNodeServlet/duepublico_derivate_00084402/Healthcare_Analytics_2025_7_100378.pdf)
headline_numbers: Experiment #1 (ChatGPT/GPT-4, 23 Mar 2023 version, one standardized prompt): primary diagnoses 85% accuracy (95% CI 62.1-96.7), secondary diagnoses 55.8% (47.8-63.5), medications 85.9% (79-91.1), allergies 100% (83.8-100); ICD-10 codes 85% primary (70% Hospital A, 100% Hospital E) and 60.7% secondary (52.7-68.2); medication dosage 83%, regimen 78.8%, ATC codes 78.8% (71.2-85.2). Experiment #2 (refined prompt, ChatGPT 24 May 2023 version): primary diagnoses 95%, secondary diagnoses 88.9%, medications 92.2%; ICD-10 secondary codes 60.7% -> 77.9%, dosages 83% -> 85.2%, regimens 78.8% -> 86.6%, ATC 78.8% -> 79.5%. Conditional on a diagnosis being identified, ICD-10 accuracy was 92.8% (116/125) in exp #1 and 86.2% (144/167) in exp #2. Open-source LLMs (StableVicuna-13B, oasst-sft-6-llama-30b) failed to fill the template in all cases. Dataset: 20 German discharge letters, 10 patients each from two hospitals.
note: Full text of the main article (11 pages) obtained and read in its entirety: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 2 Methods (2.1 Dataset, 2.2 Experiments, 2.3 Evaluation); 3 Results (3.1 Experiment #1, 3.2 Experiment #2, 3.3 Correlation of accuracy and document length, 3.4 Reproducibility); 4 Discussion (4.1 Diagnosis extraction, 4.2 Medication extraction, 4.3 Comparison with OpenSource models, 4.4 Clinical application, 4.5 Regulatory considerations, 4.6 Limitations, 4.7 Future work); 5 Conclusion; declarations; Data availability; References. CAVEAT: Appendix A (supplementary tables A.1-A.7: original German prompts, "additional metrics for both hospitals combined", example outputs, open-source failure example, Kendall's Tau table) is hosted as separate supplementary data and I could NOT retrieve it. It plausibly contains further precision/recall/F1 breakdowns, but nothing in the main text signals it contains a note-blind baseline, a classical/supervised comparator, a crossed context x capacity design, a paired significance test, or a table-provenance statement, so I do not think it changes any score. Two scores deserve explicit flagging as judgement calls. (a) Item 3 scored Y on a stage-wise conditional decomposition (ICD-10 accuracy restricted to diagnoses the model actually identified, isolating how much of the coding error is inherited from the upstream extraction stage); there is no retrieval module in this system, so no oracle-over-candidates or random-selection null exists, and a stricter reader could score this NA or N. (b) Item 8 scored Y is partial: template non-compliance is quantified only for the open-source arm ("in all cases"), whereas GPT-4's malformed outputs were repaired at run time by pressing "Regenerate response" or typing "Continue" with no frequency reported, so the headline GPT-4 accuracies are post-repair. The paper does, however, avoid coercing absent items to defaults - "missing" is its own scored category with percentages in Figs 2-5, and the allergies "Not specified" vs "None" mismatch is reported as an error in 5 cases rather than silently normalised. Item 6 scored NA because the system performs no retrieval and displays no external evidence; each letter is pasted into a fresh chat ("For each document, the first prompt is copied into a new chat followed by the document"), so cross-patient contamination is structurally impossible, but that is a property of the design rather than a provenance claim about retrieved evidence. Note also that experiments #1 and #2 differ in BOTH prompt and ChatGPT version, which the authors themselves flag as a confound ("this outcome could also be influenced by the utilization of different versions of ChatGPT in experiments #1 and #2") - this is precisely the confounded-not-crossed pattern item 5 excludes.

i1.basis: Searched §2.2 Experiments (which enumerates exactly two experiments plus the open-source LLM run), §2.3 Evaluation (which lists all metrics and statistics), §3.1-3.2 Results and §4.3 Comparison with OpenSource models. The only comparators are GPT-4's own refined prompt (experiment #2) and two other LLMs (StableVicuna-13B, oasst-sft-6-llama-30b). No constant/most-frequent-code/label-prevalence predictor that ignores the letter appears anywhere.

i2.basis: Searched §1 Introduction (which cites CRF/LSTM/BERT NER methods only as background), §2.2-2.3, §3 Results, and §4.1-4.2 Discussion (which cite ICD-coding work [35-37] and medication-extraction work [10,38-40] narratively). No TF-IDF/SVM/CNN/PLM-ICD-style baseline was re-run on the 20-letter cohort and no literature number is quoted on this benchmark; the dataset is private ('The authors do not have permission to share data').

i3.basis: "The accuracy of ICD-10 code prediction heavily depends on GPT-4's ability to first identify the corresponding diagnoses. In instances where diagnoses were recognized, the accuracy of ICD-10 code predictions was 92.8% (116 out of 125 identified diagnoses) during the first experiment and 86.2% (144 out of 167 identified diagnoses) in the second." (§4.1 Diagnosis extraction) - a stage-wise attribution separating what the diagnosis-identification stage makes available from what the coding stage does with it.

i4.basis: "To enhance clarity and reduce the overall character count, the letterhead, the footer, and the laboratory values were removed from all the discharge letters." (§2.1 Dataset); Table 1 reports a per-document "Discharge Letter Non-Whitespace count" for all 20 letters (2302-8650 characters), and Table 2 states "For each document, the first prompt is copied into a new chat followed by the document." Output truncation is also handled explicitly: "If it stopped, but the output is not complete. [prompt] Continue".

i5.basis: Searched §2.2 Experiments and §3.1-3.2. Prompt (context) and model capacity are varied one at a time, not crossed: the experiment-#1 prompt was run on GPT-4 and on the two open-source models, while the refined experiment-#2 prompt was run on GPT-4 only, and the GPT-4 version also changed between experiments (23 March 2023 vs 24 May 2023). The authors themselves note this confound in §3.2: "this outcome could also be influenced by the utilization of different versions of ChatGPT in experiments #1 and #2." No open-source x refined-prompt cell exists, so no interaction is estimable.

i6.basis: The system performs no retrieval or candidate generation and displays no retrieved evidence: each anonymised letter is pasted whole into a fresh ChatGPT session with a fixed template-filling prompt (§2.2, Table 2). There is no evidence corpus, no exemplar retrieval and no cross-note lookup, so the item cannot apply.

i7.basis: "'correct' means that the data extracted by GPT-4 is both present in the discharge letter and accurately formulated." and "'wrong context' means that the information predicted by GPT-4 is present in the discharge letter, but it is not predicted in the correct context." (§2.3 Evaluation), adjudicated externally: "The assessment of the outputs was carried out by a radiologist in his fourth year of residency for Hospital A and by a physician with 3.5 years of experience in radiology and transfusion medicine for Hospital E."

i8.basis: "Lastly, in all cases, the models failed to provide answers in the requested output template." (§4.3) and "open-source LLMs did not provide similar levels of accuracy and could not consistently fill the template" (Abstract); for GPT-4, template failures and their handling are stated explicitly - "If the codes (ATC or ICD-10) could not be correctly generated, and GPT-4 was outputting '[insert ICD-10 code here]' instead of the code, the button 'Regenerate response' was pressed" (§2.2) and "The newer version demonstrated fewer difficulties in accurately identifying and generating the desired output template, eliminating the need for additional prompts or output regeneration" (§3.2). Missing fields are not coerced to defaults: "'missing' is used to describe instances that should have been predicted, but were not" is a separately counted category reported with percentages in Figs 2-5. NOTE: no malformation RATE is given for GPT-4 itself, so this Y is partial (see note field).

i9.basis: Searched §2.3 Evaluation, which lists the complete statistical toolkit - accuracy/precision/recall/F1, Clopper-Pearson 95% CIs, Mann-Whitney U (used only to compare DOCUMENT LENGTHS between the two hospitals, p = 1.0), Shapiro-Wilk (normality), Kendall's Tau (length-vs-accuracy correlation) - and §3.1-3.4 Results. No paired test (bootstrap, permutation, McNemar, Wilcoxon signed-rank) compares systems or prompts on the same notes; the experiment #1 vs #2 gains (e.g. 55.8% -> 88.9%) and the GPT-4 vs open-source contrast are reported as raw differences with no test. The only CIs are Clopper-Pearson intervals on single systems' own rates, which the rubric excludes.

i10.basis: Searched §2.3 Evaluation, §3 Results, §4.7 Future work, Data availability and the declarations. No statement that tables or numbers are generated from stored artifacts or checked for provenance; evaluation was manual physician annotation, and §4.6/§4.7 confirm the pipeline was not automated - "necessitated the manual annotation of medications, conditions, and allergies by experienced practitioners" and "developing and implementing automated annotation and evaluation pipelines would alleviate the time and resource constraints associated with manual processing". Data availability states "The authors do not have permission to share data."
